revision.text:
Video via https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PB20HRX3H7k
A conversation between Michel Bauwens and Franz Nahrada.
=Description=
"The dialogue focus on the fundamental nature of "integral" multiperspectivity, allowing us to keep in mind the real and the imaginal at the same time, whilst focusing on the question whether after the decay and death of the industrial left and the obvious flaws of identity politics a new value system is possible that enables us to found cosmolocal politics on a cooperation of humans, nature and AI, while recognizing the spiritual dimension. "Every revolution is a revolution in value systems" is a perspective that does not replace, but enrich Marx' theory of modes of production.
Franz Nahrada analyzes the contribution of the German "value-critique" to the deciphering of the extractive nature of the "value-form" which is at the core of capitalist society. Only if we understand it completely, we will able to overcome it."
=Transcript=
Edited and improved transcripts from ChatGPT:
(Rough transcript is at [https://docs.google.com/document/d/18N2Qs7xaTaqlfd8G6b3qSE-NP_dTlwEBpli1PNvge_c/edit?tab=t.0])
==Contents==
[[Value, Labour, Commons, and the Regeneration of Life]]: A dialogue between Michel Bauwens and Franz Nahrada
Part I — Introduction: Why the Integral Left? (Michel and Franz's introductions)
Part II — The Integral Tradition and the Transformation of Value (Michel's presentation)
Part III — From Value Form Critique to Regenerative Value (Franz's response)
Part IV — Labour, Contribution, and the Future of Human Creativity (the Michel–Franz exchange)
Part V — Toward an Integral Left in the Age of AI and Ecological Crisis (concluding synthesis)
==Text==
===Part I — Introduction: Why the Integral Left?===
====Michel Bauwens====
Hello, everybody. I would like to begin by briefly explaining why we are having this conversation.
My name is Michel Bauwens. I am the founder of the P2P Foundation, and my friend Franz Nahrada is the founder of the Global Villages Network. He will introduce his own work in more detail shortly.
Franz and I have been friends for many years, but we are also engaged in an ongoing conversation about politics, strategy, and the question of how we can contribute to creating a better world. We each approach these questions from different angles, but there is a deep convergence in our concerns.
This conversation emerged from an invitation I received to give a presentation on the integral tradition and the transformation of value in relation to the early Marx. Since I was unable to attend the event in person, we decided to record this discussion independently.
Before I begin my presentation, I would like Franz to briefly introduce himself and his perspective.
====Franz Nahrada====
Thank you.
My name is Franz Nahrada. I am originally a sociologist, and I am also a hotel manager from Vienna, Austria.
As a student, I became deeply involved in politics, as well as in the critique of science and the humanities. This led me through a long intellectual journey, during which I gradually came to understand that Marxism itself needed to be deepened if it was to remain capable of helping us understand the world and develop strategies appropriate for today's complex conditions.
The point that connects my work most strongly with Michel's is what I call cosmolocalism—expressed through the idea of global villages.
The essential idea is that global and translocal connections do not necessarily weaken local communities. On the contrary, when properly organized, they can strengthen local life. Global networks can become a foundation for a renaissance of the local.
At one point, I was fortunate to receive a letter from Corinne McLuhan. She wrote that I had understood her husband's insight correctly: when global connections expand, they eventually reverse into an unprecedented renaissance of the local.
That is precisely what I have been working toward, and I believe Michel and I are ultimately engaged in a very similar project.
====Michel Bauwens====
I should add one clarification.
Neither Franz nor I would describe ourselves today as formally Marxists. However, we both take the Marxist tradition seriously, in the same way that one can engage critically with Christianity, psychoanalysis, or other major intellectual traditions without simply identifying with them.
Every tradition contains valuable insights as well as limitations. Our purpose here is not to defend a political identity, but to enter into dialogue with certain ideas that remain profoundly relevant.
The title of the original invitation was "The Rebirth of the Integral Left."
So the first question is: what does integral or integrative mean?
===Part II — The Integral Tradition: Beyond the Division of Mind and Matter===
'''Michel Bauwens'''
To explain what I mean by the integral tradition, I want to begin with the work of the radical thinker Lauren Gner, whose ideas have influenced my own reflections on what I call cosmological categories.
The basic distinction is between two fundamentally different ways of understanding reality.
The first is a dualistic worldview: the idea that reality is divided into separate realms—mind and matter, spirit and nature, subject and object.
Descartes represents perhaps the clearest expression of this tendency. This division became one of the dominant characteristics of modern Western thought.
The second approach understands reality as integrated, unified, and non-dual. In this view, mind and matter are not separate substances existing independently from one another. They are interdependent aspects of a single reality, continually co-arising and influencing each other.
According to Gner, this distinction also helps us understand different historical tendencies within Marxism and the broader left.
He argues that before the Enlightenment, the non-dual tradition remained much stronger in Europe. Renaissance thinkers did not necessarily see science, humanity, and spirituality as contradictory domains. They attempted to understand reality as a unified whole.
A figure such as Paracelsus illustrates this perspective. His medical thinking combined empirical observation with symbolic and spiritual understandings of nature. For him, these were not separate worlds but different expressions of a larger order.
This worldview was closely connected with the Hermetic tradition.
However, something fundamental changed with the Enlightenment.
The modern worldview increasingly separated mind from matter. Nature became an external object to be studied scientifically. Humanity became separated from nature, and consciousness became separated from the material world.
According to Goldner, this inaugurated what he calls a cold tradition: a tradition of separation, abstraction, and objectification.
Official Marxism, in his interpretation, partly inherited this tendency. The scientific and technological orientation of modernity became dominant within many left-wing movements, emphasizing economic structures, productive systems, and material organization.
But another tradition continued to exist beneath the surface.
The Renaissance current survived through a more hidden spiritual and philosophical lineage, culminating in figures such as Jakob Böhme, whose ideas profoundly influenced German Idealism and, through it, thinkers such as Hegel.
The young Marx, especially the Marx of the early writings, still belonged partly to this "warm" tradition. He was not only concerned with economic structures but also with alienation, human creativity, and the relationship between humanity and nature.
The integral tradition seeks to preserve this dimension.
It refuses to separate human beings from nature, consciousness from matter, or meaning from material existence. Instead, it understands humanity as an interconnected expression of a larger reality.
====Ken Wilber and Integral Theory====
A modern representative of this integrative tradition who had a major influence on me is Ken Wilber.
One of Wilber's most important contributions was his attempt to synthesize different schools of psychology and different traditions of human development.
His book The Spectrum of Consciousness addressed a fundamental problem: if we look at the enormous diversity of psychological traditions—Freud, Jung, humanistic psychology, Gestalt therapy, and others—how do we understand their relationship?
Wilber's answer was that these approaches may represent different levels or dimensions of human development. They are not necessarily mutually exclusive. Each may reveal something important from a particular perspective.
He later extended this approach to Eastern traditions of consciousness development.
Western approaches often emphasize reflection, interpretation, and conceptual understanding. Many Eastern traditions, by contrast, focus on direct observation of consciousness itself through meditation and contemplative practices.
Wilber attempted to integrate these different approaches into a larger developmental framework.
The principle that became especially important for me was his model of the four dimensions of reality.
Every phenomenon, he argued, has:
#an interior individual dimension: the "I"; #an exterior individual dimension: the "It"; #an interior collective dimension: culture and shared meaning; #an exterior collective dimension: systems and social structures.
These dimensions are all real, and none can simply be reduced to the others.
When we analyze any phenomenon, we should therefore examine all these perspectives.
For example, when studying history, we can learn from thinkers who emphasize ideas, consciousness, and human agency. We can also learn from historical materialists who emphasize economic structures, geopolitical forces, and systems of production.
The integral perspective suggests that the question of which comes first—ideas or material conditions—is often too simplistic. Reality develops through continuous feedback loops between these dimensions.
Mind and matter co-create one another.
====Integrating Perspectives====
A simple way to understand the integral approach is this:
Every perspective illuminates certain aspects of reality while leaving others in shadow.
A different perspective may reveal what the first one overlooked, while creating its own blind spots.
By combining perspectives, we do not arrive at a perfect final viewpoint, but we develop a richer and more complete understanding.
That is the foundation of the integral tradition.
===Part III — From Integral Theory to an Integral Left===
'''Michel Bauwens'''
I would now like to turn to the question of the Integral Left.
Ken Wilber is not particularly recognized within academic circles, but his influence has been enormous. His books circulate widely throughout the world, and his ideas have influenced many people working in fields such as architecture, organizational theory, technology, and social innovation.
Thinkers such as John Vervaeke, Brendan Graham Dempsey, and others have engaged deeply with Wilber's work—sometimes extending it, sometimes criticizing it, but always responding to it as an important intellectual reference point.
However, it is important to recognize that the integral movement associated with Wilber was not originally a left-wing or Marxist movement.
In many ways, it emerged from a Californian intellectual culture: entrepreneurial, individualistic, and often oriented toward personal development and organizational transformation.
This does not make it unimportant. But it does mean that the integral tradition, by itself, is not automatically connected to emancipatory politics.
At one point, however, there was an attempt to develop a more progressive interpretation of integral theory.
After Ken Wilber founded the Integral Institute, a small group of people within that broader movement began exploring what an integral political perspective might look like. I was part of that group, together with people such as Michael Brooks, Greg Wilpert, and others.
It was never a large movement, and ultimately it did not develop into a major current. The wider integral movement moved in different directions, often toward more centrist or conservative interpretations.
Eventually, I also moved away from that framework.
Looking back, however, I realize that the P2P Foundation was in many ways my own attempt to develop an Integral Left.
The approach of the P2P Foundation is based on identifying and strengthening what I call seed forms: existing social practices that already contain the potential forms of a future society.
Rather than imagining transformation only as a complete rupture with the existing system, we look for emerging forms of cooperation, commons-based production, and peer-to-peer organization that already exist within the present.
These practices are the seeds from which a different social order may grow.
====Rethinking Left and Right====
'''Michel Bauwens'''
I would also like to say something about the meaning of left and right.
A very narrow understanding sees the left as the political expression of the industrial working class, with the labour movement seeking to transform capitalism, while the right seeks to preserve existing social and economic structures.
But historically, the situation is much more complex.
The original modern left was actually the left wing of the bourgeois French Revolution. The term referred simply to the seating arrangement within the revolutionary assembly. It did not initially refer to socialism or the labour movement.
The meanings of left and right have constantly changed.
Reading Carroll Quigley's The Evolution of Civilizations influenced my thinking about this question. Quigley interpreted historical conflicts—such as those between Catholic traditions and secular or rationalist movements—as expressions of deeper tensions between different social orientations.
My own interpretation is that the difference between left and right is ultimately connected to the question of the circle of care.
The right tends to begin from the community that already exists: family, nation, culture, tradition, or a particular social group. Its priority is often to protect and strengthen that community.
The left begins from an impulse to expand the circle of belonging and responsibility.
It asks:
How far can we extend our concern?
Only to our own group?
To all human beings?
To other forms of life?
To the living Earth itself?
This tension is probably a permanent feature of human societies. It reflects something deeply rooted in human psychology.
People themselves often move along this spectrum during their lives. A person may be more radical and expansive when young and become more conservative later.
Therefore, when I speak of an Integral Left, I do not mean simply a revival of twentieth-century socialism, classical Marxism, or even liberal progressivism.
I mean the emergence of a new form of emancipatory politics adapted to a world transformed by artificial intelligence, ecological crisis, and new forms of social organization.
The fundamental question remains the same:
Do we expand our circle of care, or do we not?
====The Value Revolution====
'''Michel Bauwens'''
This leads me to the final part of my argument: the question of value.
I would argue that every major revolution in history has also been a revolution of value.
Consider the ancient world.
In ancient Greece and Rome, labour was generally considered a low form of activity because much of it was performed by slaves. The ideal citizen was not someone who worked, but someone who participated in political life, philosophy, and civic affairs.
To call a free citizen a labourer would have been an insult.
Christianity transformed this understanding.
The principle of ora et labora—prayer and work—gave labour a new dignity. Human work became participation in the ordering and renewal of creation.
This was connected to a broader integration of matter and spirit. Human beings were not merely spiritual beings trapped in a material world; embodied life itself had meaning.
The great monotheistic traditions—Judaism, Christianity, and Islam—are deeply social religions. They emphasize responsibility within the world, not escape from it.
This represented a genuine value revolution.
Labour became meaningful. The worker became a person with spiritual dignity.
====From Land to Labour to Commodity====
A further transformation occurred in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
The physiocrats argued that value originated primarily from land.
Later thinkers such as Adam Smith, David Ricardo, and Karl Marx argued that labour was the foundation of value.
Capitalism, however, transformed this further by organizing value around commodities.
The commodity became the dominant form through which value was measured and exchanged.
But today, I believe we are facing another transformation: a new value revolution.
The emerging peer-to-peer and commons movements point toward a different foundation: contributory value.
The question is no longer only:
How much can we extract?
The question becomes:
How can we contribute to the regeneration of the systems that make life possible?
====From Extraction to Regeneration====
Since the Neolithic revolution and the emergence of money, human economies have largely been organized around extraction.
Resources are extracted, transformed into commodities, monetized, taxed, and partially redistributed.
Regeneration comes afterward.
But this creates a structural imbalance: regeneration depends upon prior extraction.
I believe the coming value revolution requires reversing this relationship.
Extraction will remain necessary. Human beings need food, shelter, and material resources.
But extraction must become subordinate to regeneration.
Economic activity must be organized according to the long-term ecological health of the planet.
====Contributory Value and the Commons====
Examples of contributory value already exist.
Peer production communities, especially free software communities, have developed ways of recognizing contributions that are invisible to traditional markets.
They create systems of recognition and sometimes alternative forms of accounting for people who contribute outside conventional employment.
But I believe the transformation goes deeper.
Even if money continues to exist, monetary creation itself will eventually need to become connected to ecological regeneration.
We can already measure ecological conditions:
#Is soil quality improving? #Is biodiversity recovering? #Are water systems becoming healthier? #Is the atmosphere improving?
A future monetary system could be based not on the expansion of extraction, but on measurable improvements in the health of living systems.
The logic would be reversed.
Instead of regeneration depending on extraction, extraction would become dependent on regeneration.
===Part IV — From Value-Form Critique to Regenerative Value===
'''Franz Nahrada'''
Thank you, Michel.
When you invited me to contribute to the PORTALOOZA festival discussion on the young Marx, I thought: yes, we should go back to the foundations and take a closer look. We arrive at many similar conclusions, but it is important to examine more closely how we arrived there.
There are still many people operating within a traditional Marxist framework. That framework has important strengths, but also clear limitations. For me, reconsidering the very nature of value within capitalist society is one of the essential questions.
I would like to begin with a theoretical influence that shaped my thinking very early.
I owe a great deal to my first teacher, Volkbert Michael Roth aka Mike Rot, from Constance. In 1974, he invited a group of around thirty people to a seminar on the theory of cognition. It was a very important experience for me because he argued that '''we can only understand how we understand reality by applying our methods to a concrete example'''.
His example was Marx's Capital. His book had just come out: https://doc1.bibliothek.li/abb/A030429.pdf
He showed us that Capital itself could be understood as a model for analysing an object: capitalism. What was fascinating was the way Marx gradually moves from abstractions toward increasingly concrete determinations, bringing different aspects of reality into the correct relationship.
Capitalism is not understood by looking at isolated facts. It requires a movement through different levels of abstraction.
The central thesis that emerged from this approach was that the best way to analyse capitalism is to analyse it as a system of forms of value. Forms that necessarily emerge as value becomes the dominant mode of productuion.
Many people who read the first chapter of Capital encounter Marx's discussion of the commodity, the value form, the relative form of value, and the equivalent form. They often find this abstract and difficult, and then move on to what appear to be more concrete issues: exchange, money, labour, and capital.
But this is a mistake.
Understanding the nature of value itself is the only way to understand what money and capital actually are.
That was my theoretical starting point in 1974.
====From Value-Form Analysis to Value Critique====
Later, after my involvement in academic criticism, I came into closer contact with a current that did not call itself value-form analysis, but '''value critique'''.
This was the German tradition that emerged from the journal '''Marxist critique''' and was later associated with the journals Krisis and Exit!, especially through thinkers such as Robert Kurz and others. See article on Wertkritik in this Wiki: https://wiki.p2pfoundation.net/Wertkritik
I want to emphasize this because the theme of this conference is the young Marx.
For this reason, I would like to begin with a relatively unknown text by the young Marx: the James Mill excerpts.
This text is not part of the standard Marx-Engels collected works in the usual editions. It is found in the MEGA edition—the Marx-Engels-Gesamtausgabe—which contains the complete body of Marx's writings.
https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/download/Marx_James_MIll.pdf
Why do I consider this text so important, perhaps even more important than the better-known Paris Manuscripts?
Because in his confrontation with James Mill, an apologetic defender of capitalism, Marx makes a fundamental observation:
There is no such thing as harmonious exchange under capitalism.
Marx uses very strong language. What appears on the surface as a process of mutual benefit is, in reality, a process of reciprocal appropriation.
His argument is essentially this:
If I could simply take what I wanted from another person directly, I would do so. But because direct appropriation is socially unacceptable, capitalism provides an economic mechanism through which appropriation takes place indirectly.
In this sense, capitalism becomes a system of mutual appropriation through economic means.
Behind the apparent equality of exchange lies a relationship in which each party attempts to extract as much as possible from the other:
#paying as little as possible; #receiving as much as possible; #maximizing one's advantage within market relations.
Therefore, from the very beginning, value under capitalism appears not as a harmonious social relationship, but as an extractive relationship.
====The Commodity as Double Abstraction====
This is where Robert Kurz made an extremely important contribution.
Traditional Marxism often reads the opening pages of Capital in a simplified way.
It sees commodities as having:
#a positive aspect: use value, meaning usefulness; #a negative aspect: exchange value, meaning their role as objects of market exchange.
According to this interpretation, use value represents the authentic human side of production, while exchange value represents the distortion introduced by capitalism.
Kurz argued that this is not sufficient.
The problem is deeper.
Under capitalism, even use value is already shaped by the logic of value accumulation.
The issue is not merely that exchange corrupts otherwise innocent production. Rather, the production of wealth itself is organized from the beginning around the expansion of abstract value.
Even usefulness becomes abstract.
A commodity appears as something useful for an isolated consumer.
But behind this apparently simple relationship lies an enormous network of relations that disappear from view:
#forests and ecosystems; #soil and water systems; #knowledge accumulated over generations; #commons and cooperative practices; #unpaid care work; #the metabolic relationship between human beings and nature.
All of this disappears behind the seemingly simple question:
"What quality makes this object useful to me?"
The commodity is therefore not only one abstraction.
It is a double abstraction.
As exchange value, it reduces the richness of the world to quantities of abstract labour.
As use value, it reduces the richness of the world to abstract utility for an isolated individual consumer.
In both cases, the living relationships that constitute real wealth disappear from view.
====Beyond Extraction: Regenerative Wealth====
A regenerative economy—or a contributory economy, whatever term we choose—cannot simply produce different commodities.
The problem is not only what commodities contain. The problem is the economic form itself.
We therefore need a different understanding of wealth.
Wealth is not the accumulation of objects, nor the accumulation of monetary power over objects.
Real wealth lies in the flourishing of relationships:
#between people; #between communities; #between humanity and the living Earth.
The value of a forest is not exhausted by its timber.
The value of knowledge is not exhausted by its market price.
The value of care is not exhausted by its wage.
Their essential contribution lies in their ability to sustain and regenerate the conditions of life itself.
This is why the distinction between extractive and contributive—or regenerative—value reaches far beyond economics.
It points toward a civilizational transformation:
#from valuing what can be extracted #to valuing what enables life to reproduce and flourish.
Only from this perspective can we begin to imagine a post-capitalist theory of value.
Capitalism measures value according to what can be extracted.
A regenerative society would recognize value according to what can be regenerated.
====Toward an Integral Left====
This also points toward the possibility of a renewed integral left.
For more than two centuries, much of the left shared with liberal modernity a similar underlying ontology:
#nature as an external object; #society as the primary arena of history; #production as the defining human activity.
But we are now reaching the limits of that worldview.
Artificial intelligence and robotics force us to ask a fundamental question:
What is the place of the human being in a world where machines can increasingly perform productive tasks?
Historically, the struggle was primarily about who should own and distribute the products of labour, or who should control the means of production.
But the deeper question was often left untouched:
How is life itself reproduced?
A regenerative perspective changes the focus.
Human labour is only one element within much larger processes:
#ecological regeneration; #social reproduction; #cultural creation; #cognitive development.
Wealth does not emerge from labour alone.
It emerges from living systems that continuously reproduce the conditions under which labour, knowledge, and society can exist at all.
====Marx Revisited====
This does not mean abandoning Marx.
On the contrary, I believe it radicalizes Marx.
Marx recognized the commodity as the elementary form of social wealth under capitalism. Therefore, beginning our analysis with the commodity remains essential.
But we must extend the critique.
The issue is not only the extraction of surplus labour from workers.
It is also the extraction of:
#soil fertility; #biodiversity; #care; #knowledge; #communities;
... and ultimately the regenerative capacities of the Earth itself.
An integral left would therefore no longer define emancipation simply as the liberation of labour.
It would define emancipation as the liberation of life's capacity to regenerate itself.
====Conclusion====
The young Marx envisioned communism as the restoration of humanity's conscious relationship with its own social nature, beyond the fetishism of the commodity.
Today, in the age of ecological breakdown, this vision must be expanded once more.
It must become the conscious regeneration of the web of life of which humanity itself is a part.
===Part V — Labour, Contribution, and Human Creativity===
'''Michel Bauwens'''
Thank you, Franz.
I would like to return to the question of labour, because I think this is one of the points where we may have a slight difference in emphasis.
For me, the concept that replaces labour is contribution.
I have been influenced here by the work of Benjamin Suriano, whose dissertation From Modes of Production to the Resurrection of the Body explores the historical and spiritual dimensions of labour, particularly the Christian idea of labour as a salvific activity.
Suriano emphasizes something very important: in the Christian tradition, labour was not simply economic production.
The monks, for example, created communities of production. Their life was not only about consumption or withdrawal from the world. They cultivated land, produced food, created beautiful things, and organized collective life.
Their labour became an expression of the integration of spirit and matter.
It represented the idea that human beings participate consciously in the renewal and ordering of the world.
The Reformation, however, changed this relationship.
By transforming wealth into a sign of divine grace and accepting the commodification of labour, it contributed to a degradation of labour into an economic category.
Marx, in a certain sense, attempted to recover labour as a source of human emancipation.
But I believe this is the point where the traditional Marxist framework reaches its limits.
Labour under capitalism remains trapped within capitalist categories.
One possible socialist response was to take over the industrial system and manage it differently. This was the approach of actually existing socialism.
Another response was to negotiate a larger share of the wealth produced by the system.
But both approaches still operate within the framework of labour as the central organizing principle.
I believe something new is emerging.
Within capitalism itself, we can already see the emergence of another mode of production based on:
#contribution; #commons; #peer production; #collaborative creation.
The people who contribute to the commons are, in a sense, engaged in a new form of salvific labour—not labour in the capitalist sense, but contribution toward the regeneration of the Earth.
====The Social Contract Beyond Humanity====
I see the future as involving a new relationship between three major forces:
#the living world; #humanity; #artificial intelligence.
AI should not be understood as an autonomous replacement for humanity. It should be understood as a mediating technology that helps us perceive and manage complexity.
But for this future to work, we need to expand our social contract in two directions.
First, we need a renewed social contract among human beings.
Every person should have access to basic conditions of life:
#healthcare; #housing; #security; #the ability to participate in society.
But we also need to extend the social contract beyond humanity.
We need to recognize our relationship with the living world itself.
The natural systems that sustain us cannot continue to be treated merely as resources available for extraction.
We need a partnership with the Earth.
This is why I believe contribution and regeneration are becoming central categories for the future.
=====Franz Nahrada=====
I understand your argument, Michel, and I think we are very close.
But I want to defend something important about labour.
During our preparatory conversations, I mentioned that my thinking developed through several stages, including discussions with people who were critical of the idea that we should simply abandon the concept of labour.
I think there is a danger in throwing away this concept too quickly.
Marx himself gives an important example in the fifth chapter of Capital: the comparison between the bee and the architect.
The bee can build an extraordinary structure—the beehive.
But the difference is that the beehive does not exist in the mind of the bee before it is created.
The human being, by contrast, can imagine, anticipate, and consciously plan a result before producing it.
This is the essential point.
The core of labour is not manual effort.
The core of labour is the uniquely human capacity for conscious anticipation.
Marx sometimes referred to this as the activity of the "total productive labourer."
Labour is not fundamentally about physical exertion.
It is about the ability to create according to an imagined purpose.
Labour as the Activity That Reduces Necessity
A very beautiful definition of labour that I encountered is this:
Labour is the human activity that constantly diminishes its own necessity.
This captures something essential.
Machines and tools are not created merely to save labour in the narrow sense.
Human creativity develops techniques, instruments, and processes that reduce unnecessary toil and open space for new capacities.
What disappears on one side—the burden of repetitive manual activity—must be rebuilt on the other side through greater intellectual, creative, and social capacities.
The problem is that industrial society has continuously destroyed this higher dimension of labour.
It separates people from knowledge.
It removes their ability to understand and participate in the processes that create the world around them.
This is why I find the work of thinkers such as Frithjof Bergmann important.
At the end of his life, Bergmann argued that we must reorganize human productive capacities independently from capital.
For me, this remains a profoundly emancipatory perspective.
=====Michel Bauwens=====
I completely agree with the point about anticipation and creativity.
In my own vocabulary, I would perhaps call this orchestration.
Human beings have the capacity to organize complexity, to imagine possible futures, and to coordinate different elements into meaningful wholes.
So I do not believe labour disappears.
The question is rather whether labour remains the dominant social category within capitalism.
This is where I think the transformation occurs.
In one of our preparatory conversations, Franz, you said something that I found extremely powerful:
"We are evolving toward a world where capital does not need labour and labour does not need capital."
I think this captures something fundamental.
====Technology, Knowledge, and the Struggle Against Cognitive Proletarianization====
Michel Bauwens:
Another thinker who has influenced me deeply is Bernard Stiegler, the philosopher of technology who wrote the preface to one of my books.
Stiegler emphasized two central ideas.
The first is negentropy.
Humanity's task is not simply to produce more, but to counteract entropy: the degradation of ecological systems, social relations, and knowledge.
The second concerns what he called the proletarianization of knowledge.
In the nineteenth century, workers lost craft knowledge because machines incorporated their skills.
Today, something even broader is happening.
Cognitive capacities themselves are being externalized.
We risk creating a world where:
3humans no longer know how things work; #humans no longer need to understand; #artificial systems controlled by capital accumulate the knowledge.
This is the new form of proletarianization.
The challenge is therefore to deproletarianize knowledge.
The people building new technological infrastructures today are often motivated precisely by this goal: to regain control over their tools, their production systems, and their knowledge.
We need technologies that serve human autonomy rather than technologies that concentrate power.
=====Franz Nahrada=====
Yes, and I think this brings us very close.
The question is not whether labour exists or disappears.
The question is whether human beings regain control over their creative capacities.
A future society cannot simply eliminate production. It must transform the relationship between human creativity, technology, and the living world.
====Closing Reflection====
The conversation between Michel Bauwens and Franz Nahrada reveals two complementary paths toward an integral left.
One path emphasizes the emergence of contribution, commons, and regenerative value beyond labour as the central economic category.
The other emphasizes the recovery of labour as conscious, creative, anticipatory human activity beyond its capitalist reduction to wage work.
Both perspectives reject the idea that the future can simply be a continuation of industrial modernity.
Both recognize that the deepest transformation concerns not only ownership or distribution, but the very meaning of value, wealth, technology, and humanity's relationship with the Earth.
The question for an integral left is therefore not merely:
Who owns production?
It is also:
* What kind of relationship do human beings wish to create with each other, with technology, and with the living world that sustains them?

'''* Article: Value, Labour, Commons, and the Regeneration of Life: A dialogue between Michel Bauwens and Franz Nahrada. August 2026.'''
Improved transcript of a dialogue from the video: [[Rebirth of the Integral Left]] [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PB20HRX3H7k]
=Text=
= The Rebirth of the Integral Left: Value, Labour, Commons, and the Regeneration of Life =
'''A dialogue between [[Michel Bauwens]] and [[Franz Nahrada]]'''
== Context ==
This dialogue took place in the context of a discussion originally prepared for the PORTALOOZA festival. Michel Bauwens had been invited to present on the theme of the "rebirth of the integral left", with a particular focus on the integral tradition and the transformation of value in relation to the early writings of [[Karl Marx]].
Since Bauwens could not attend the event in person, the conversation was recorded independently with Franz Nahrada, founder of the [[Global Villages Network]], joining as a dialogue partner.
Although neither participant identifies formally as Marxist, both engage critically and constructively with elements of the Marxist tradition. Their conversation brings together several intellectual currents:
* integral theory; * Marxian critique; * value-form critique; * commons-based peer production; * contributory value; * regenerative economics; * ecological and technological transformation.
The central question of the dialogue is how an emancipatory politics can respond to a world transformed by ecological crisis, artificial intelligence, and new forms of social organization.
== Introduction: Why an Integral Left? ==
=== Michel Bauwens ===
Michel Bauwens introduces the conversation by explaining that he and Franz Nahrada have long shared an interest in politics, strategy, and the search for pathways toward a better world.
Bauwens is the founder of the [[P2P Foundation]], while Nahrada is the founder of the [[Global Villages Network]]. Although their approaches emerged from different intellectual traditions, both are concerned with forms of social transformation that strengthen cooperation, local autonomy, and global connection.
The original invitation to Bauwens concerned the relationship between the integral tradition, the transformation of value, and the early Marx. The purpose of the dialogue is therefore not to defend a particular political identity, but to explore how different traditions of thought can contribute to a renewed emancipatory perspective.
=== Franz Nahrada ===
Franz Nahrada introduces himself as originally trained in sociology and based in Vienna, Austria. His intellectual development was shaped by involvement in political critique, as well as criticism of science and the humanities.
For Nahrada, Marxism contains important insights but also requires deepening in order to address the complexity of contemporary society.
A central concept connecting his work with that of Bauwens is '''cosmolocalism''', expressed through the idea of '''global villages'''.
The principle of cosmolocalism is that global connections do not necessarily weaken local communities. When organized appropriately, translocal networks can strengthen local capacities and create a renaissance of local life.
Nahrada refers to an insight associated with [[Marshall McLuhan]]'s work: that the expansion of global connections may ultimately lead not to the disappearance of locality, but to an unprecedented renewal of the local.
== The Integral Tradition: Beyond the Division of Mind and Matter ==
=== The Dualistic and Non-Dual Views of Reality ===
Bauwens begins his presentation by exploring the meaning of the term '''integral''' or '''integrative'''.
Drawing on the work of Lauren Gner, he distinguishes between two broad ways of understanding reality.
The first is a dualistic worldview, in which reality is divided into separate domains:
* mind and matter; * spirit and nature; * subject and object.
[[René Descartes]] represents a major expression of this tendency in modern Western thought. This separation became a dominant feature of modernity, where nature increasingly came to be understood as an external object available for scientific analysis.
The second approach understands reality as integrated and non-dual.
From this perspective:
* mind and matter are not independent substances; * spirit and nature are not separate worlds; * human beings and the natural world exist within a relationship of mutual emergence.
Reality is understood as a unified process in which different dimensions co-arise and influence each other.
=== The Warm and Cold Traditions ===
According to Gner's interpretation, the Renaissance preserved elements of this integrative worldview.
Renaissance thinkers often combined:
* scientific inquiry; * humanistic reflection; * spiritual understanding.
Figures such as [[Paracelsus]] did not necessarily see physical science and symbolic or spiritual knowledge as contradictory. They belonged to a tradition influenced by [[Hermeticism]], in which reality was approached as a unified whole.
The Enlightenment introduced a decisive change.
Nature became increasingly understood as an external object separated from human consciousness. Mind and matter became distinct categories, and scientific analysis increasingly operated through abstraction and separation.
Gner describes this as the emergence of a '''cold tradition'''.
Within this interpretation, parts of modern Marxism inherited this tendency through their emphasis on scientific analysis, productive systems, and material structures.
However, another tradition continued beneath the surface: a '''warm tradition''' emphasizing integration, human creativity, and the relationship between humanity and the larger living world.
This current continued through figures such as [[Jakob Böhme]] and influenced German Idealism, including the intellectual environment in which the young [[Karl Marx]] developed.
For Bauwens, the integral tradition seeks to preserve this dimension:
* humanity is not separate from nature; * consciousness is not separate from material existence; * social transformation cannot be understood only through economic structures.
The integral perspective therefore attempts to reconnect dimensions that modernity separated.
== Ken Wilber and Integral Theory ==
Bauwens identifies [[Ken Wilber]] as one of the most influential modern representatives of the integrative tradition.
Although Wilber is not widely recognized within academic philosophy, his work has had a significant influence across many fields, including psychology, architecture, organizational theory, and social innovation.
His book '''The Spectrum of Consciousness''' attempted to synthesize different schools of psychological thought.
=== Integrating Psychological Traditions ===
Wilber's starting point was the observation that different psychological traditions often appeared to contradict one another:
* [[Sigmund Freud]] and psychoanalysis; * [[Carl Jung]] and analytical psychology; * humanistic psychology; * Gestalt therapy; * human potential movements.
Rather than treating these approaches as mutually exclusive, Wilber interpreted them as describing different dimensions or stages of human development.
Each tradition could reveal something important from a particular perspective.
The question was therefore not which approach was simply correct, but rather:
* At what level of development does a particular approach become meaningful? * What aspect of human experience does it illuminate? * What are its limitations?
=== Integrating Eastern and Western Traditions ===
Wilber later extended this approach to Eastern traditions of consciousness development.
Bauwens emphasizes the distinction between many Western and Eastern approaches.
In Western traditions, reflection often means deep examination of concepts, texts, and ideas.
Many Eastern traditions, by contrast, focus on direct observation of consciousness itself through practices such as meditation.
Wilber attempted to integrate these different traditions into a broader developmental framework.
=== The Four Dimensions of Reality ===
One of Wilber's most important contributions for Bauwens is the idea that every phenomenon contains four dimensions.
These dimensions can be represented as four interconnected perspectives:
* '''The interior individual dimension ("I")''' ** consciousness; ** subjective experience; ** personal development.
* '''The exterior individual dimension ("It")''' ** the physical body; ** technological objects; ** observable processes.
* '''The interior collective dimension ("We")''' ** culture; ** shared meanings; ** collective worldviews.
* '''The exterior collective dimension ("Its")''' ** institutions; ** economic systems; ** organizational structures.
For Bauwens, this framework provides a useful heuristic for analysing social reality.
No single dimension should automatically be considered the ultimate determining factor.
Human consciousness influences social structures, but social structures also influence consciousness. Technology shapes society, but society also shapes technology.
Reality emerges through continuous feedback relationships.
=== The Integration of Perspectives ===
Bauwens summarizes the integral approach through the metaphor of light and shadow.
Every perspective illuminates certain aspects of reality while leaving others unseen.
A different perspective may reveal what was hidden by the first perspective, while creating its own limitations.
The purpose of integrating perspectives is therefore not to eliminate disagreement, but to achieve a richer and more complex understanding of reality.
This is the foundation of the integral tradition.
== From Integral Theory to an Integral Left ==
=== The Political Question of Integration ===
Bauwens then turns to the question of how integral thinking relates to politics.
He emphasizes that the integral movement associated with Wilber was not originally a Marxist or left-wing tradition.
The broader integral movement developed largely within a Californian intellectual environment associated with:
* personal development; * organizational transformation; * alternative culture; * entrepreneurial approaches.
While this movement produced important insights, it was not intrinsically connected to the emancipatory traditions of socialism or the labour movement.
=== The Attempt to Develop an Integral Left ===
Within the broader integral movement, a small group attempted to develop a more progressive political interpretation.
Bauwens was briefly involved in this current, together with thinkers including Michael Brooks, Greg Wilpert, and others.
The group explored whether integral theory could contribute to a renewed emancipatory politics.
However, it remained a small current, and the broader integral movement developed in other directions, often becoming more associated with centrist or conservative interpretations.
Bauwens therefore moved away from the integral movement as such.
Nevertheless, he considers the P2P Foundation to have been, in part, an attempt to develop an '''integral left''' through a different path.
=== The P2P Foundation and Seed Forms ===
The approach of the P2P Foundation is based on identifying and strengthening what Bauwens calls '''seed forms'''.
Seed forms are existing social practices that already contain elements of a possible future society.
Rather than imagining transformation only as a complete rupture, this approach looks for emerging forms of cooperation already developing within the present.
Examples include:
* commons-based peer production; * open knowledge systems; * collaborative digital infrastructures; * new forms of social cooperation.
The strategy is to recognize, protect, and expand these emerging forms.
Social transformation is therefore understood as the cultivation of possibilities already present within society.
== The Meaning of Left and Right ==
Bauwens argues that the distinction between left and right should not be understood only through modern industrial politics.
A narrow interpretation defines the left as the political expression of the labour movement seeking to transform capitalism, while the right represents those seeking to preserve existing economic and social arrangements.
Historically, however, these categories have changed.
The original modern left was the left wing of the French Revolution, referring to seating positions within the revolutionary assembly. It did not initially refer to socialism or the working class.
The meaning of left and right has continually evolved.
=== Expanding the Circle of Care ===
For Bauwens, the deeper distinction concerns the question of the '''circle of care'''.
The right tends to begin with an existing community:
* family; * nation; * cultural tradition; * established social group.
Its primary concern is often the protection and flourishing of that community.
The left begins from an impulse to expand the circle of belonging and responsibility.
The question becomes:
* Does concern extend only to one's own group? * To all human beings? * To other forms of life? * To the Earth as a living system?
From this perspective, the tension between left and right reflects a deep human and psychological structure.
A person may become more expansive and universalist at one stage of life and more protective or conservative at another.
=== The Integral Left in the Age of AI ===
The integral left, according to Bauwens, should not simply reproduce the historical left of the twentieth century.
It must respond to a fundamentally different situation:
* artificial intelligence; * ecological crisis; * new forms of production; * changing relationships between humans and technology.
The central question remains:
'''Do we expand our circle of care, or do we not?'''
For Bauwens, this question will remain central regardless of the future economic system.
== The Value Revolution: From Extraction to Regeneration ==
=== Every Revolution Is a Revolution of Value ===
Bauwens argues that every major historical transformation has also been a transformation in the understanding of value.
A revolution does not only change institutions and political structures. It changes what societies consider meaningful, productive, and valuable.
=== Labour and Value in the Ancient World ===
Bauwens begins with the example of ancient Greece and Rome.
In classical societies, labour was often considered a low-status activity because much of it was performed by slaves.
The ideal citizen was not primarily defined as a worker, but as someone dedicated to:
* political participation; * philosophy; * civic life.
To identify a free citizen with labour would have been considered degrading.
The meaning of work therefore changed profoundly with Christianity.
=== Christianity and the Transformation of Labour ===
The Christian principle of '''ora et labora''' ("pray and work") transformed the status of labour.
Work became more than economic necessity. It became a way through which human beings participated in the ordering and renewal of creation.
This was connected to a more integrated understanding of matter and spirit.
The human body and material existence were no longer understood as inferior domains separated from spiritual meaning.
The monastic tradition represented a form of collective production:
* communities cultivated land; * produced food; * created knowledge; * built and maintained places of beauty and meaning.
Labour became connected to responsibility, creativity, and participation in a larger order.
Bauwens argues that this represented a genuine '''value revolution'''.
=== From Land to Labour to Commodity ===
A further transformation occurred in early modern economic thought.
The physiocrats argued that value originated primarily from land.
Later economists, including [[Adam Smith]], [[David Ricardo]], and [[Karl Marx]], emphasized labour as the source of value.
Capitalism introduced another transformation.
Value became increasingly organized around the commodity form.
The commodity became the dominant expression through which social wealth was measured and exchanged.
However, Bauwens argues that another transformation is now emerging.
=== The Emergence of Contributory Value ===
According to Bauwens, the commons movement and peer-to-peer production indicate the emergence of a new value logic:
'''contributory value'''.
This represents a shift away from a system primarily based on extraction toward one based on contribution and regeneration.
Examples already exist within commons-based communities.
In many peer-production communities, including free software communities:
* contributions are recognized outside traditional market mechanisms; * people collaborate without conventional employment relationships; * systems emerge to value participation and collective creation.
These practices represent early forms of a different value system.
=== Extraction and Regeneration ===
Bauwens argues that human economies have historically been organized around extraction.
The general sequence has been:
# extraction of resources; # transformation into commodities; # monetization; # taxation and redistribution; # attempts at ecological repair.
However, this structure creates a fundamental imbalance.
Regeneration depends upon extraction.
The system must first extract value before it can attempt to restore ecological and social conditions.
Bauwens argues that the coming value revolution requires reversing this relationship.
Extraction must become subordinate to regeneration.
Human beings will continue to require:
* food; * shelter; * materials; * energy.
But these activities must be organized according to the long-term health of planetary systems.
=== Regenerative Value ===
A regenerative economy does not ask only:
'''How much value can we extract?'''
It asks:
'''How can we contribute to the systems that make life possible?'''
This requires a new relationship between economic activity and ecological conditions.
Possible indicators include:
* improvement of soil quality; * restoration of biodiversity; * healthier water systems; * reduction of ecological degradation.
The creation of economic value would become increasingly linked to measurable regeneration rather than extraction.
The logic would therefore be reversed:
Instead of regeneration depending on extraction, extraction would become dependent on regeneration.
=== The Commons and the Future of Value ===
For Bauwens, the commons represent practical examples of this emerging transformation.
Commons-based communities demonstrate that social value can be created through:
* cooperation; * contribution; * shared knowledge; * collective stewardship.
The challenge is to develop economic and technological systems that support these emerging forms rather than subordinating them to extractive models.
This transformation forms one of the foundations of what Bauwens calls an integral left.
== Value-Form Critique and Regenerative Value ==
=== Franz Nahrada: Returning to the Nature of Value ===
Franz Nahrada begins his contribution by explaining that his interest is not to abandon Marx, but to return to some of the deeper questions within Marx's own analysis.
When he was invited to contribute to the discussion on the young Marx, he proposed going back to the foundations of Marx's theory of value.
Although Michel Bauwens and Nahrada arrive at many similar conclusions, Nahrada emphasizes a different route: a closer examination of the value form itself.
For Nahrada, the essential question is:
'''What is the nature of value in a capitalist society?'''
=== The Influence of Value-Form Analysis ===
Nahrada recalls the influence of an early teacher who introduced him to Marx's method of analysis through the example of *Capital* - Volkbert Michael Roth aka Mike Rot.
The important lesson was that Marx's analysis does not begin with concrete social phenomena immediately.
Instead, Marx begins with abstractions and gradually reconstructs the complexity of reality.
The analysis of capitalism must therefore begin with its fundamental forms.
For Nahrada, the most important of these is the value form.
Many readers of [[Karl Marx]]'s *Capital* encounter the first chapter's discussion of:
* commodity; * use value; * exchange value; * the relative and equivalent forms of value.
However, these concepts are often considered too abstract and then abandoned in favour of more familiar themes such as money, exchange, and labour.
Nahrada argues that this is a mistake.
'''The nature of value is the key to understanding:'''
* money; * capital; * commodity production; * social relations under capitalism. * the capitalist state.
=== Value Critique and the Krisis Tradition ===
Nahrada later became connected with currents of Marxian critique that went beyond traditional Marxism.
In particular, he refers to the German tradition associated with:
* value-form analysis (Mike Rot); * value critique (Robert Kurz); * the journal [[Krisis]].
see: https://wiki.p2pfoundation.net/German_Marxist_Value_Critique
This current argued that capitalism should not be understood only as a system of unequal distribution.
The deeper problem lies in the social forms through which value itself is produced.
The question is therefore not only:
'''Who receives the wealth created by capitalism?'''
but also:
'''What kind of social reality is created when wealth itself is organized through value accumulation?'''
=== The Young Marx and the James Mill Excerpts ===
Nahrada emphasizes a relatively less discussed text of the young Marx:
the '''James Mill Excerpts'''.
This text is found in the [[Marx-Engels-Gesamtausgabe]] (MEGA), the complete critical edition of Marx and Engels' works.
Nahrada considers this text particularly important because it reveals Marx's early critique of the idea that capitalist exchange is a harmonious process.
In the conventional economic view, exchange appears as a relationship of mutual benefit:
* two parties voluntarily exchange goods; * both gain from the transaction; * exchange creates cooperation.
However, Marx's analysis in the James Mill excerpts presents a much more conflictual interpretation.
Exchange is not simply cooperation.
It is a form of reciprocal appropriation.
Behind the appearance of equality, each participant attempts to obtain the maximum advantage from the other.
The economic relationship therefore contains an element of mutual extraction.
=== Value as an Extractive Social Relation ===
From this perspective, value is not neutral.
Value under capitalism represents the attempt to produce something that embodies socially recognized labour and can function within processes of accumulation.
The problem is not merely that capitalism distributes value unfairly.
The deeper issue is that the production of wealth itself is organized according to the logic of accumulation.
This leads Nahrada to the work of [[Robert Kurz]], one of the central thinkers of the value-critique tradition.
=== The Commodity as Double Abstraction ===
Nahrada explains that traditional Marxist interpretations often distinguish between:
* use value, understood as the useful qualities of things; * exchange value, understood as the monetary or market dimension.
From this perspective, use value appears positive and natural, while exchange value appears as the problematic capitalist distortion.
Robert Kurz challenged this interpretation.
The problem is not simply that exchange value corrupts an otherwise innocent production process.
Rather, both dimensions of the commodity are already shaped by capitalist abstraction.
The commodity represents a '''double abstraction'''.
==== Exchange Value as Abstraction ====
As exchange value, the commodity reduces the richness of the world to quantities of abstract labour.
Complex social and ecological relations become represented through numerical exchange relations.
==== Use Value as Abstraction ====
But use value is also abstracted.
A commodity appears simply as something useful for an individual consumer.
Behind this apparently simple usefulness disappear the wider relationships that make the object possible:
* forests; * soils; * rivers; * accumulated knowledge; * collective cooperation; * unpaid care work; * ecological systems.
The commodity hides the living networks from which it emerges.
=== Beyond Commodity Wealth ===
A regenerative economy cannot therefore simply produce different commodities.
The problem is not only the content of commodities, but the economic form itself.
A post-capitalist theory of value must begin with a different understanding of wealth.
True wealth is not:
* the accumulation of objects; * the ability to purchase more commodities; * the expansion of monetary value.
Rather, wealth consists in the flourishing of relationships:
* between human beings; * between communities; * between humanity and the living Earth.
The value of a forest is not exhausted by its timber.
The value of knowledge is not exhausted by its market price.
The value of care is not exhausted by wages.
Their deeper contribution lies in their capacity to sustain and regenerate the conditions of life.
== From Extraction to Regeneration: A Civilizational Shift ==
=== Beyond the Critique of Exploitation ===
Nahrada argues that the distinction between extractive and regenerative value represents more than an economic reform.
It points toward a civilizational transformation.
Capitalism organizes value according to what can be extracted, accumulated, and exchanged.
A regenerative society would organize value according to what can be sustained, renewed, and expanded.
The question therefore shifts from:
'''How much can be extracted from the world?'''
to:
'''What enables life to continue flourishing?'''
=== Expanding Marx's Critique ===
For Nahrada, this perspective does not abandon Marx.
Rather, it radicalizes Marx's own starting point.
Marx identified the commodity as the elementary form of capitalist wealth.
Following this insight, the critique must begin with the commodity itself and the social relations embedded within it.
However, the critique must now be expanded.
The issue is not only the extraction of surplus labour from workers.
It also concerns the extraction of:
* soil fertility; * biodiversity; * ecological stability; * knowledge; * care; * community; * the regenerative capacities of the Earth itself.
An integral left would therefore redefine emancipation.
It would no longer mean only:
'''the liberation of labour'''
but also:
'''the liberation of life's capacity to regenerate itself.'''
=== The Future of the Integral Left ===
Nahrada argues that much of the historical left shared assumptions with liberal modernity.
These included:
* nature as an external object; * society as the primary arena of historical development; * production as the defining human activity.
However, this worldview is now reaching its limits.
The emergence of:
* artificial intelligence; * robotics; * ecological breakdown;
forces a deeper reconsideration of the human role.
The historical struggle focused largely on:
* who owns production; * who controls the means of production; * how the products of labour are distributed.
The future challenge concerns a deeper question:
'''How are the conditions of life itself reproduced?'''
A regenerative perspective recognizes that human labour exists within larger systems of regeneration:
* ecological systems; * social relationships; * cultural traditions; * cognitive processes.
Humanity does not create wealth alone.
We participate in living systems that make all human activity possible.
== Labour, Contribution, and Human Creativity ==
=== Michel Bauwens: Contribution as the Emerging Category ===
Bauwens returns to the question of labour.
He explains that for him, the emerging category that replaces labour as the central organizing principle of value is:
'''contribution'''.
Drawing on the work of Benjamin Suriano and his study '''From Modes of Production to the Resurrection of the Body''', Bauwens reflects on the historical meaning of labour.
Suriano emphasizes the Christian idea of '''salvific labour'''.
In early Christian communities, particularly monastic communities, labour was not simply economic production.
It was a way of integrating:
* spiritual life; * material activity; * collective responsibility.
Monastic communities represented forms of collective production:
* cultivating land; * producing food; * creating beautiful environments; * organizing shared life.
Labour became an expression of participation in the renewal of the world.
=== The Transformation of Labour Under Capitalism ===
According to Bauwens, the Reformation transformed this relationship.
By connecting wealth with divine approval and accepting the increasing commodification of labour, it contributed to reducing labour to an economic category.
Marx later restored labour to a central position by identifying it as the source of human emancipation.
However, Bauwens argues that this framework is no longer sufficient.
Labour under capitalism remains embedded within capitalist categories.
Historical socialism largely attempted to:
* take control of industrial production; * manage the existing productive system differently.
But this still preserved labour as the central organizing principle.
=== The Emergence of Commons-Based Contribution ===
Bauwens argues that a new mode of production is already emerging within capitalism.
This new mode is based on:
* commons; * peer production; * contribution.
The contributors who create and maintain commons represent a new social force.
Their activity is not primarily organized around wage labour.
Instead, it is oriented toward:
* shared resources; * collective knowledge; * ecological and social regeneration.
Bauwens describes this as a contemporary form of salvific contribution: activity directed toward sustaining the living world.
=== The Expanded Social Contract ===
Bauwens proposes that the future requires a new social contract involving three interconnected dimensions:
* humanity; * the living world; * artificial intelligence.
The first dimension concerns the traditional social contract among human beings.
Every person should have access to:
* healthcare; * housing; * basic security; * participation in society.
The second dimension extends this contract beyond humanity.
Human beings must recognize their interdependence with:
* ecosystems; * other species; * natural processes.
The third dimension concerns AI.
Artificial intelligence should function as a mediating technology that helps humanity manage complexity, rather than becoming a system of domination controlled by capital.
=== Franz Nahrada: Defending the Creative Dimension of Labour ===
Nahrada responds that while he agrees with much of Bauwens' argument, he wants to preserve the concept of labour.
He argues that there is a danger in abandoning the term too quickly.
For Nahrada, labour contains a unique human capacity that should not be confused with capitalist wage labour.
The central issue is not manual activity.
It is conscious creation.
=== The Bee and the Architect ===
Nahrada refers to Marx's famous example from the fifth chapter of *Capital* comparing the bee and the architect.
The bee can construct a complex structure.
However, the crucial difference is that the structure does not exist in the bee's consciousness before it is produced.
The architect, by contrast, imagines and plans the result before creating it.
The defining characteristic of human labour is therefore:
* anticipation; * imagination; * conscious organization of activity.
Labour is not fundamentally physical effort.
It is the capacity to create according to a consciously formed purpose.
== Labour as the Reduction of Necessity ==
=== The Human Capacity to Transform Work ===
Nahrada continues by arguing that labour should not be understood primarily as physical effort or as the activity imposed upon workers under capitalism.
The essential characteristic of labour is the uniquely human ability to imagine, anticipate, and consciously create.
He refers to a definition of labour that he finds particularly meaningful:
'''Labour is the human activity that constantly diminishes its own necessity.'''
This expresses an important paradox.
Human beings create tools, techniques, and social forms that reduce the amount of necessary effort required for survival.
The purpose of technology should therefore not simply be to increase productivity.
Its deeper purpose is to free human capacities for higher forms of creativity, cooperation, and understanding.
=== The Development and Destruction of Human Capacities ===
Human history can be understood as a process in which labour gradually reduces unnecessary toil.
What disappears on one side — repetitive and exhausting manual activity — should create space on the other side for:
* creativity; * knowledge; * cooperation; * cultural development.
However, Nahrada argues that industrial society has often moved in the opposite direction.
Rather than expanding human capacities, industrial organization has frequently separated people from knowledge.
People increasingly lose understanding of the processes through which their world is created.
Production becomes something performed by specialized systems rather than something consciously understood and participated in.
=== Frithjof Bergmann and the Reorganization of Work ===
Nahrada refers positively to the work of [[Frithjof Bergmann]], who argued that society must reorganize human productive capacities independently from capital.
For Nahrada, this represents an important emancipatory perspective.
The goal is not to eliminate human productive activity.
The goal is to liberate human creativity from the structures that reduce it to wage labour.
== Michel Bauwens: Labour, Contribution, and Orchestration ==
Bauwens responds that he agrees with Nahrada's emphasis on anticipation and creativity.
The difference is mainly one of terminology and emphasis.
Bauwens describes this human capacity as '''orchestration'''.
Human beings have the ability to:
* organize complexity; * coordinate different elements; * imagine possible futures; * create meaningful systems.
In this sense, Bauwens does not argue that human creativity disappears.
Rather, he questions whether labour should remain the central category through which society understands value.
=== A World Where Capital Does Not Need Labour and Labour Does Not Need Capital ===
Bauwens recalls a phrase from his earlier conversation with Nahrada that he considers particularly insightful:
'''We are evolving toward a world where capital does not need labour and labour does not need capital.'''
This expresses a fundamental transformation.
Traditional industrial capitalism created a relationship of dependence:
* capital required labour; * labour required access to capital.
New technological and social conditions may make possible forms of production where human creativity can operate outside traditional capitalist structures.
The challenge is to build the infrastructures that allow this possibility to develop.
== Technology, Knowledge, and the Future of Human Capacity ==
=== Bernard Stiegler and Negentropy ===
Bauwens introduces the work of [[Bernard Stiegler]], a philosopher of technology whose ideas strongly influenced his thinking.
Stiegler emphasized the concept of '''negentropy'''.
Entropy refers to the tendency toward disorder and degradation.
Human civilization has always involved the creation and maintenance of forms of order:
* ecological; * social; * cultural; * technological.
Humanity's task is therefore not simply production, but the active management of complexity and the struggle against destructive forms of entropy.
=== The Proletarianization of Knowledge ===
A second major concern of Stiegler's work is what Bauwens describes as the '''proletarianization of knowledge'''.
In nineteenth-century industrialization, workers lost craft knowledge as machines incorporated previously human skills.
However, contemporary capitalism extends this process further.
Today, not only manual skills but also cognitive capacities are increasingly externalized.
The danger is the emergence of a world in which:
* humans no longer understand how things function; * knowledge becomes concentrated in technological systems; * artificial intelligence is controlled by capital.
The result would be a society where humans lose autonomy over their own capacities.
=== Deproletarianizing Knowledge ===
For Bauwens, the struggle of the future is therefore not only about economic ownership.
It is also about recovering human knowledge and creative capacity.
This means creating technologies and infrastructures that allow people to:
* understand their tools; * participate in production; * control knowledge systems; * collaborate through open networks.
The purpose of new technological development should be the expansion of human autonomy, not the concentration of power.
== Toward an Integral Left in the Age of AI and Ecological Crisis ==
The dialogue between Bauwens and Nahrada suggests that the emergence of an integral left requires moving beyond older political categories.
The central challenge is not simply the redistribution of industrial production.
It is the transformation of the relationship between:
* value; * labour; * technology; * ecology; * human creativity.
Both speakers argue that humanity is entering a period in which the old assumptions of industrial modernity are becoming inadequate.
=== Beyond Ownership Alone ===
The historical left focused primarily on questions of:
* ownership; * class; * control of production.
These questions remain important.
However, the ecological crisis reveals a deeper problem.
The issue is not only who controls production.
It is also:
'''What forms of production sustain or destroy the conditions of life?'''
=== Toward Regenerative Civilization ===
An integral left would therefore combine several dimensions:
* social emancipation; * ecological regeneration; * technological autonomy; * restoration of human creativity; * expansion of the circle of care.
It would understand humanity not as separate from nature, but as one expression of a larger living system.
Technology, including artificial intelligence, would not be viewed simply as a threat or a solution.
Its role would depend on the social relations that organize it.
A technology controlled by extractive systems can deepen alienation.
A technology organized through commons and cooperation can expand human capacities.
=== The Final Question ===
The deepest question raised by the dialogue is therefore not only economic.
It concerns the kind of relationship humanity wishes to create:
* with itself; * with other forms of life; * with technology; * with the Earth.
The rebirth of the integral left would mean moving from a politics centred only on distribution toward a politics of regeneration.
It would mean transforming the meaning of value itself:
from what can be extracted,
toward what can contribute to the flourishing of life.
== References ==
* Marx, Karl. *Capital: Critique of Political Economy*. * Marx, Karl. *James Mill's Elements of Political Economy (Excerpts)*. * Kurz, Robert. Works on value critique and the critique of capitalist social forms. * Wilber, Ken. *The [[Spectrum of Consciousness]]*. * Stiegler, Bernard. Works on technology, knowledge, and negentropy. * Suriano, Benjamin. *[[From Modes of Production to the Resurrection of the Body]]*. * Bergmann, Frithjof. Works on new work and human productive autonomy. * McLuhan, Marshall. Works on global communication and the renewal of locality.

revision.text:
'''* Report: The Stablecoin Toolkit: Part II — Law, Regulation, and Monetary Policy. The Wharton Blockchain and Digital Asset Project (BDAP).'''
URL = https://bdap.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Final_Stablecoin-Toolkit-Regulatory-Report-2.pdf
=Description=
"Part I mapped the financial and market dimensions of stablecoins; Part II follows that heterogeneity into the domains that determine how stablecoins are actually used: private law, financial regulation, and monetary policy. Its central claim is that the same design choices separating one stablecoin from another, namely reserve composition, redemption mechanics, and custody architecture, are exactly what determine how each is treated under law and policy.
Three findings stand out. On private and commercial law, the report traces how “control” has emerged as the functional equivalent of possession for digital assets. On regulation, the report documents genuine convergence: the US (GENIUS Act), EU (MiCA), UK, Japan, Singapore, Hong Kong, and UAE had each arrived independently at a similar regulated instrument, a fiat-referenced token redeemable at par and fully backed by segregated reserves, though algorithmic, crypto-collateralized, and synthetic designs remain largely outside these frameworks. On monetary policy, the report examines how reserve-backed stablecoins resembling narrow banking affect central bank reserve access, deposit competition, and currency substitution as dollar-denominated stablecoins circulate globally.
The report closes with policy recommendations across all four areas and detailed appendices mapping regulatory and bankruptcy treatment across major jurisdictions."
(https://bdap.wharton.upenn.edu/wharton-bdap-launches-its-second-report-on-stablecoins-addressing-the-legal-regulatory-and-monetary-policy-aspects/)
