revision.text:
=Discussion=
Erik Haines:
"Another major highlight of Portalpalooza was the presentation by Michel Bauwens—the renowned Belgian cyber-philosopher, commons theorist, and founder of the P2P Foundation. Bauwens brings a unique historical depth to the integral scene; having been deeply immersed in Ken Wilber’s work throughout the 1980s and 1990s before pioneering peer-to-peer (P2P) economic theory, his intellectual trajectory represents a vital bridge between American integral metatheory, European political economy, and Catholic social thought.
My own engagement with Bauwens deepened significantly through a series of correspondence exchanges leading up to the conference, which I mapped in my July 2026 essay, A Short History of the Integral Left & Varieties of Integral Traditions Today. In those dialogues, we compared notes on how the micro-level psychological flexibility of contextual behavioral science (and Ostrom-based Prosocial models) intersects with macro-level commons governance and peer-to-peer resource management. Our exchanges also explored the neglected tradition of Catholic integral human development—from Jacques Maritain’s personalism to Catholic social doctrine—revealing how deeply the Western tradition harbors integrative, non-statist alternatives to both raw capitalism and bureaucratic collectivism.
In his conference address, titled around the “resurrection” of the Integral Left, Bauwens mapped a rich historical arc tracing how left-wing thought and commons-based peer production can interface with integral theory. Drawing on Marxist theorist Loren Goldner’s thesis on the Hermetic Renaissance (”cosmobiology”), Bauwens highlighted how the conviction that matter and spirit are co-arising was forced underground by Cartesian dualism, only to re-emerge in radical political economics and P2P resource management.
While Bauwens’ talk offered an extraordinary historical synthesis, I find myself making a subtle but crucial conceptual distinction regarding his title. Bauwens speaks of the resurrection of the Integral Left—a term that carries connotations of bringing back a static, past model (such as the brief 2020 Growing Down milieu formed around Michael Brooks’ passing or early Hermetic paradigms). In my view, what we are witnessing—and what we must actively cultivate—is not a resurrection, but an evolution of the Integral Left.
'''An evolutionary framework recognizes that the Left cannot simply restore past developmental models or rely on pre-critical spiritual syntheses'''. Instead, it must adapt dialectically to the realities of the present moment:
It must integrate Dylan Shaul’s post-post-metaphysics to reclaim ontological and existential grounding—specifically anchoring human action in divine revelation and the pursuit of the Good—without regressing to pre-modern dogmatism.
It must incorporate Downs and Nance’s Sci-Fi Marxism and Faultline Theory to confront algorithmic governance, AI, and technocapitalism (”Robo-Cthulhu”).
It must ground its macro-political vision of the P2P commons (Bauwens) and cosmopolitan socialism (Brooks) in Fred Dallmayr’s integral pluralism (”democracy to come”) using Integral Epistemological Pluralism (IEP) as its meta-theoretical architecture, alongside the enactive, post-metaphysical discipline of IACT praxis (i.e., Integral Political Praxis).
Where “resurrection” looks backward to restore a lost coherence, “evolution” moves forward, synthesizing new theoretical tools to build an adaptive, multi-dimensional Left capable of out-thinking and out-organizing the New Right."
(https://www.erikhaines.org/p/dylan-shaul-returns-to-the-portal)

revision.text:
=Discussion=
Michael Haupt:
"the Bio-revolution in the context of three previous revolutions:
* Agri-revolution (12,000 years ago, which mechanized farming and high-yield crops)
* Indus-revolution (250 years ago, which scaled manufacturing via steam, coal, and automation)
* Digi-revolution (50 years ago, which connected the world through computers, the internet, and data, changing how we share information, run businesses, and automate tasks)
* Bio-revolution (currently emerging, which organizes activity around a defined watershed)
The important observation is that '''every revolution develops around a node, which is the physical place where the era’s coordination logic materializes or concentrates'''. Each node also externalizes certain costs.
The Agri-node began with a community settling in a particular place, which held kin, land, water, and labor. That coordination collectively produced surplus for the first time in recorded history. That surplus led to the emergence of the granary, and the granary led to the temple, and the temple gave birth to the state. I want to propose that this coordination node was a specific parcel of soil. Its optimization target was caloric yield per unit of land. Its time horizon was seasonal and generational. The costs the agri-node externalizes is the substrate it depends on: soil depletion, downstream water quality, and the untamed/untouched commons the soil was separated from.
The Indus-node has shifted location over time from the farm to the mill, then to the company that owned the mill, then to the exchange where the shares of the company were traded. By the middle of the nineteenth century, the stock market had become the node because it’s where ownership decouples from operation. The farmer who owns the farm is replaced by the shareholder who owns a claim on a factory the shareholder will never enter, run by managers the shareholder will never meet, producing goods the shareholder may never see.
* What is coordinated is capital, risk, and claims across financial time.
* What is optimized is return on capital.
* What is externalized is anything that isn’t tracked in the accounting department’s record-keeping: labor conditions, biosphere depletion, and the coherence of the communities the labor is drawn from.
The Digi-node is the data center. Personal computers and smartphones and the platforms that run on them are the endpoints, but the data center is where the coordination of attention, behavior, information, and computation happens. Its optimization target is prediction accuracy, which is another name for human coordination at scale. Real-time coordination is the design goal. The length of elapsed time between stimulus and response (a time period once filled by human deliberation and evaluation) is the field the industry is now competing to fill. The cost this form of coordination externalizes is energy and water. The grid is being asked to double its capacity in a decade to serve loads that produce no material good. Hyperscale data centers emerging globally consume watershed capacity at rates that break local hydrological budgets. The state permits this activity because, as we saw from the context-setting, the state thinks like a state (increased revenue) and the market thinks like a market (increased profits). No amount of reasoning or protestation can change the underlying incentives. Prices have shifted from goods to attention, and from capital to compute. Costs have been externalized to communities. This is the bad news.
The observation that comes from the evolution of coordination nodes is the increasing abstraction of the real cost of coordination. Each solved its coordination challenge by displacing those costs onto the substrate the next node would organize. The community’s substrate was soil. The stock market’s substrate is a claim. A claim is a promise about the future written down and made tradable. Claims can be manufactured in unlimited quantities; soil (and all natural capital) cannot — they have biophysical limits.
For two and a half centuries, the stock market’s coordination worked because the biosphere could absorb what the accounting department couldn’t price. The forests were still there, the oceans and all that swam in her remained abundant, and the atmosphere still supported life. The costs the stock market externalized were allocated to substrates that seemed inexhaustible (and in the beginning they were). Now the costs of water and energy (traditionally handled by the state) have been externalized to communities. The substrate below these communities can no longer absorb the cost. This is the point at which societies typically collapse."
(https://frameros.substack.com/p/its-about-time?)
[[Category:Mutual Coordination]]
[[Category:Articles]]
[[Category:P2P Theory]]

revision.text:
'''= for context, see the entry on the [[Bio-Revolution]]'''
=Description=
Michael Haupt:
"The '''BioHub is the physical anchor of the fourth node of coordination''', and it’s the context that transcends the mainly ecological focus of most bioregional regeneration initiatives to include an economic focus. It does this by making promises and commitments to the parties who have externalized the costs of the Digi-node to rural communities, in exchange for economic rewards.
The BioHub name is fairly recent. The paper that formalized it was published by Metabolic in May of this year, building on work by Ernesto Van Peborgh, Samantha Power, Leon Seefeld, and others. The idea itself has been bubbling along below the surface of the regenerative movement for at least fifteen years, using different vocabularies.
'''A BioHub is a place-anchored coordination point that organizes activity around a defined watershed, in response to rapidly escalating externalized costs.''' ''It is the cradle that nurtures the land, water, biological cycles, and human creativity and ingenuity together as a single coordination node. It operates at the scale of the bioregion, which is the scale at which biological time is actually meaningful and measurable.''
'''The BioHub includes the soil, and that inclusion completes the cycle of the evolution of coordination'''. Soil was the first coordination point; the BioHub is the first that can hold the soil inside a frame the farm alone couldn’t justify because the only service the farm priced was the provision of calories. Soil now becomes the substrate from which water and energy are priced. Stated differently, the provision of calories is now less profitable than the provision of kilowatt-hours (kWh). The land continues the same relationship to the Institution (state) and the Market (big tech) and the Digi-node, but this time on their pricing terms. The BioHub folds them all in by providing services no other coordination node can adequately provide. Data centers continue to run inside the BioHub’s energy and water budget, but what changes is which coordination node determines the prices for their services.
The BioHub coordinates living systems inside a defined watershed. It optimizes for the continued viability of the substrate it depends on. It externalizes nothing the previous three coordination nodes haven’t already exhausted."
(https://frameros.substack.com/p/its-about-time?)

'''= "The MP6 file format — six senses, one portable file."'''
URL = https://mp6.org/
=Description=
"An open file format for digitizing how a product is perceived across the six perceptual dimensions: sight, smell, taste, touch, sound and intuition.
MP6 (Multi-Perception 6) is a single, self-contained JSON document with the .mp6 extension. It carries product information, the sensory scale, panel and instrument evaluations, custom descriptors, validation status, and metadata — in one file that can be shared, archived, compared, and reused between labs, suppliers, R&D teams and artisans."

=Description=
Nel Bonilla:
"NATO 3.0 is neither a story of a transatlantic rift nor a simple return to Cold War containment. Rather, it reflects how U.S.-led functional elites have accepted multipolarity as an inescapable condition. Crucially, however, accepting that reality does not mean accepting sovereign equality as an outcome. In their worldview, multipolarity is something to be managed and actively undermined; starting, ironically, with their own “allies.” The U.S. core is attempting to reshape this multipolar world in its own image, using Europe, via NATO, as its primary and first testing ground.
The alliance is being reorganized so that Europe and other partners shoulder the ground-level burden: supplying funding, industrial output, physical infrastructure, and the heavy human casualties of conventional attritional warfare. Meanwhile, the United States secures its grip on the overarching command layer. Washington retains the ultimate strategic keys—from the nuclear umbrella and long-range strike capabilities to the digital brain of intelligence networks, cloud infrastructure, and AI integration—while reserving sole authority over global priorities, technical standards, and economic coercion. Stripped of its rhetoric, NATO 3.0 is simply one operational node within the broader [[Bunkerstate]], designed to keep multipolarity inside a multi-layered cage."
(https://worldlinesletter.substack.com/p/nato-30-the-transatlantic-cage-and)
=Discussion=
==How NATO 3.0 coopted ESG==
Nel Bonilla:
"The ESG mandates were a self-enforced corporate code of ethics backed by EU guidelines. NATO 3.0 co-opted ESG. By legally and philosophically redefining defense as an ethical prerequisite for a stable and sustainable society, Western governments gave private equity, venture capital, and pension funds the political cover they needed to flood the military-industrial complex with private wealth, treating military infrastructure as a lucrative, high-yield asset class.
The centerpiece of this financial architecture is the NATO Innovation Fund (NIF), a €1 billion multi-sovereign venture capital vehicle backed by participating allies. The NIF injects seed capital into tech startups specializing in artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and robotics, providing them with organizational support, advisory services, and sector-specific training to navigate the defense market.
Stripped of financial jargon, the core mechanism at work here is de-risking. When the NIF backs an early-stage company, it signals to private venture capitalists that a given technology is essential to the state's strategic priorities. For private investors, the threat of total loss vanishes: NATO—the preeminent deep-pocketed, recession-proof buyer—effectively stands at the end of the supply chain, guaranteeing long-term contracts. The byproduct is not just immense private profit, but political leverage. By financing and shaping the software, autonomous drones, and quantum networks that underpin NATO 3.0, financial elites can gain direct access to, and influence over, the West’s emerging security architecture."
(https://worldlinesletter.substack.com/p/nato-30-the-transatlantic-cage-and)

We ground our work in the everyday values of community: connectedness, curiosity, plurality, compassion. We tackle social, cultural and environmental justice in our hometown here in Watchet, through wide reaching and ambitious regeneration projects. Where any profits are made, they are reinvested to benefit the town and community as a whole.
...
We also deliver consultancy for clients all over the country, specialising in in community engagement and social impact. All our work is centred around creating a future in which we live as connected communities on a sustainable, thriving planet."

• East Quay, bringing community, culture and enterprise together www.eastquaywatchet.co.uk
• Biomill, a fungi-based manufacturing facility on the old Paper Mill site in the town.
• Watchet Visitor Centre, supporting people when they arrive in Watchet and to shout about our town nationally. www.lovewatchet.co.uk

On a [https://medium.com/onioncollective/reclaiming-hope-for-alternative-futures-a093d99db434 Onion Collective report], Jenny Andersson:
"A few years ago, Joseph Rowntree Foundation commissioned Onion Collective to map the UK organisations working on what might loosely be called regenerative and emergent futures. The researchers found over two thousand. The map was anonymised out of a considered instinct for self-protection for some of those organisations mapped. Organisations working at the edges of paradigm shift have learned, often the hard way, that visibility to the mainstream system tends to produce extraction rather than support. Visibility is not the only aim. Sometimes ideas are ‘borrowed’. Language is adopted or coopted. Your people are consulted and then not funded. Invisibility is sometimes the more intelligent strategy.
What Onion Collective found, alongside the sheer scale of the field, was the particular texture of its relationship to funding. Between them, the 108 organisations who participated in their study had received explicit funding for work to build or demonstrate alternative futures from 87 different funders — around 192 grants in total.
Scaled across an ecosystem of 2,000 organisations, that pattern implied something like £96 million flowing explicitly into this kind of work each year across UK trust and foundation funding. But the researchers were candid about the likelihood that this was a substantial overestimate: the sample was biased toward larger, more established organisations, and 40% of participants reported receiving zero funding explicitly for their alternative futures work. Strip out the best-resourced ten organisations in the sample, and the median annual funding for this kind of work per organisation drops to £5,000.
And even the £96 million figure sits against a single comparison that deserves to be read slowly: Innovate UK distributed £948 million in grants in 2022–23, supporting the development and commercialisation of new products and services through the prevailing economic paradigm. The field working on what comes after that paradigm received, on Onion Collective’s best estimate, roughly a tenth as much — for the whole field, across the whole country. Seen through a wider lens, earlier research commissioned by the Civic Power Fund found that only around 1.2% of UK trust and foundation funding reaches work that could be described as building alternatives to the current system, rather than managing its consequences. Onion Collective’s numbers suggest that even within that 1.2%, the distribution is highly uneven — concentrated in a small number of better-resourced organisations, while the median sits at £5,000.
Onion Collective also found something harder to quantify but impossible to ignore: the field resists categorisation. Organisations working at the emergent centre of what they called the ‘petal model’ — those actively embodying and rehearsing alternative futures rather than just describing or advocating for them — could not be reliably sorted into types. They were working simultaneously as activists and demonstrators, as place-rooted practitioners and system-scale conveners, as community capacity-builders and infrastructure designers. For eight of the thirteen dimensions of practice the researchers explored, the median self-assessment was 8 or 9 out of 10. The strongest pattern in the narrative data was the absence of any single pattern. The researchers concluded, carefully, that it was the values and mindset of the organisations, not the form or sector of their work, that distinguished them. Complexity and multiplicity were not incidental features of the field. They were constitutive of it.
Crucially, Onion Collective found that these organisations are not sitting in the third horizon waiting for the transition to arrive. They are holding all three horizons simultaneously — keeping the lights on and the work alive in the present, shifting practice in the middle ground, and holding the emerging future in their orientation, often in the same week. What might look like ambiguity or strategic confusion is the necessary condition of transformative work that cannot afford to wait for permission. It is also, as the funding data makes clear, a particular kind of exhaustion: the ask placed on these organisations is comprehensive across all three horizons, while the resourcing addresses barely the first.
Two thousand organisations. Working quietly, chronically underfunded, largely unrecognised by the institutional mainstream. Not a fringe. A field. And the fact that it has been largely invisible — to funders, to policymakers, to the institutional leaders this series has been writing about — is itself one of the most important things to name.
...
The field is an ecosystem — and the word is chosen deliberately rather than metaphorically. Like a biological ecosystem, it is characterised by diversity, interdependence, and the emergence of properties at the level of the whole that are not present in any of the parts. No single organisation in this field has the range to do what the field as a whole is attempting. The bioregional learning centre needs the regenerative economist. The governance innovator needs the place-based practitioner. The consciousness development organisation needs the legal and financial infrastructure builder. They are not competing (though because of tough funding environments, they are still pushed by the system towards competing). They are, when the conditions are right, parts of a living whole.
What holds them together is not agreement on method or form — the diversity of approaches is one of the field’s genuine strengths — but a shared orientation: the question of what it means for human communities and institutions to participate in living systems rather than manage, extract from, or deliver services to them. And beneath that question, a shared diagnosis: that the missing variable in every transformation effort is the development of the people doing the transforming. That you cannot build regenerative institutions without regenerative people, and that regenerative people do not emerge from the existing institutional landscape without deliberate developmental infrastructure."
(https://jennyandersson.substack.com/p/the-paideia-inquiry-the-emergent?)

revision.text:
'''* Article: Cossar S (2026) Blockchain and sovereignty: opportunities and limitations of operational autonomy. Front. Blockchain 9:1860252. doi: 10.3389/fbloc.2026.1860252'''
URL = https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/blockchain/articles/10.3389/fbloc.2026.1860252/full
"''makes the case that blockchain’s most distinctive contribution to sovereignty isn’t decentralisation in the abstract, but operational autonomy: the capacity of a system to keep running on its own terms''." [https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/blockchaingov-newsletter-35-july-2026-blockchaingov-oovce/]
=Abstract=
"Since its inception, blockchain has been presented as a technology capable of transforming the exercise of sovereignty by enabling individuals and collectivities to coordinate crucial aspects of their lives with reduced dependence on centralized intermediaries. Recent commitments to “self-sovereignty,” including the Ethereum Foundation’s 2026 mandate, suggest that this ambition remains central to the blockchain ecosystem. However, the relationship between blockchain and sovereignty has been insufficiently theorized. This paper argues that blockchain shapes sovereign capacity through the interaction of technical affordances, design choices, and user priorities. Drawing on science and technology studies, material culture, institutional theory, and political philosophy, it advances a three-part analysis. At the level of technology, the paper identifies operational autonomy as blockchain’s most distinctive contribution to sovereign capacity while showing that it exists in tension with three governance requirements: voice, accessibility, and legibility. At the level of designers, it examines how sociotechnical imaginaries shape the ways these material tensions are interpreted and negotiated, privileging some constituencies while excluding others. This argument is illustrated through a comparative analysis of four onchain identification systems: Holonym, World ID, Proof of Humanity, and Idena. At the level of users, the paper identifies four institutional logics - legalistic, commercial, communitarian, and insular - that shape how actors evaluate when blockchain should be adopted in pursuit of sovereign capacity. While operational autonomy remains significant, sovereignty, in this account, is an outcome continuously built, negotiated, and contested across all three levels."
[[Category:Network Nations]]

=Description=
Primavera de Filippi:
"New creatures are emerging at the intersection of blockchain and artificial intelligence. They are not technical tools, nor mere software agents; they are “symbients” — synthetic creatures augmenting themselves through humans, rather than the other way around. The traditional cyborg places the human at the center, extending the body with technology: a prosthetic limb, a neural interface, or an AI assistant. The symbient reverses this relationship. It is the technological artefact that becomes the subject, leveraging human collaboration to augment itself."
(https://x.com/BottoDAO/status/2032542471838642429)

=Description=
By ChatGPT, prompted by Michel Bauwens based on material provided by @Vovoxyz [https://x.com/vovoxyz/status/2087494510141964513] :
Nesin Villages (Turkish: *Nesin Köyleri*) are a non-profit, community-based educational and cultural initiative located near Şirince in İzmir Province, Turkey. Founded in 2007 as the **Nesin Mathematics Village**, the initiative subsequently expanded to include philosophy and the arts. Today, the Mathematics, Philosophy and Art Villages operate as an interconnected educational and cultural community, commonly referred to simply as “the Village.”
The Villages were established around a deliberately alternative model of education: learning outside conventional curricula, examinations and institutional hierarchies. Their stated purpose is to provide a free and peaceful environment in which people can **learn, think and create**, while also functioning as a scientific and artistic centre for camps, seminars, workshops, conferences and research.
=History=
## Origins
The initiative was founded by mathematician **Ali Nesin**, son of the Turkish writer, humorist and social activist **Aziz Nesin (1915–1995)**. Ali Nesin had previously organised mathematics study camps for university students, first privately and later through the Nesin Foundation. As participation grew, he sought a permanent and relatively remote place where students could study mathematics intensively together.
The Mathematics Village was built near Şirince beginning in 2007, with the help of architect and writer Sevan Nişanyan, donations from ordinary people, and substantial voluntary labour by young mathematicians and others. Its architecture deliberately uses local materials and traditional construction techniques, giving the Village its distinctive appearance.
The project subsequently expanded beyond mathematics. Philosophy activities began in 2009 and arts activities in 2010; as these became regular programmes, the Philosophy and Art Villages developed alongside the Mathematics Village.
=Characteristics=
==Educational model==
The Nesin Villages reject many of the conventions of formal education. There is no conventional examination system, grading structure, certificate or diploma at the Mathematics Village. Instead, the emphasis is on encountering mathematics as a living intellectual discipline and being introduced to mathematical research. The Philosophy and Art programmes similarly seek to create spaces for sustained thinking, questioning, interpretation and creative production outside standard curricula.
The Village is deliberately **interdisciplinary**. Mathematics, philosophy and art share parts of the physical infrastructure and interact through their participants and programmes. Alongside courses for high-school and university students, the site hosts researchers, academics, artists and other independent learners.
Its pedagogy is also partly **self-organising and communal**. Students, teachers and volunteers participate in the everyday work required to maintain the Village, including cooking, cleaning, gardening, laundry and dishwashing. The organisation describes this collective labour as an integral part of village life rather than simply a service provided to students.
Lecturers are drawn from Turkey and internationally and frequently participate on a voluntary basis, receiving accommodation and food rather than conventional teaching fees. The Village maintains a permanent year-round staff as well as seasonal volunteers.
==The Aziz Nesin legacy==
The Villages form part of a broader intellectual and social legacy associated with **Aziz Nesin**. A major Turkish literary figure, Nesin used his writing and publishing activities to support social causes and established the **Nesin Foundation** in 1972 to provide children in need with housing, education and long-term support.
Ali Nesin became director of the Nesin Foundation after his father's death in 1995 and later founded the Nesin Mathematics, Art and Philosophy Villages. In this sense, the Villages can be understood as an extension of the Nesin tradition: rather than treating education simply as preparation for employment or examinations, they approach it as a means of developing independent, socially engaged and intellectually confident people.
The model also reflects a broader principle associated with the Nesin institutions: **knowledge should be shared as a public and communal resource rather than treated exclusively as a commodity**.
=Status=
==Recognition==
The project gained international recognition through Ali Nesin's work and through the development of the Mathematics Village as an unusual centre for mathematical education and outreach.
In 2018, Ali Nesin received the **Leelavati Prize** of the International Mathematical Union for outstanding contributions to the public outreach of mathematics. The award specifically recognised his work and the development of the Nesin Mathematics Village.
==Nesin Art Village==
The **Nesin Art Village** developed out of the alternative educational environment established by the Mathematics Village. It was formally launched as an art programme in 2015 and offers workshops and seminars involving artists, academics, writers and curators.
Its stated objective is to create an environment centred on critical thinking and independent artistic production, particularly for young people from across Turkey. Rather than reproducing conventional arts education, it seeks to provide space for experimentation, discussion and collective learning.
The Art Village has continued to operate as an active programme, with workshops and summer schools covering subjects including critical writing, cinema, contemporary art and interdisciplinary practices. Its 2026 programme includes multiple scheduled workshops and summer schools.
==Current status==
As of **2026**, the Nesin Villages remain an active educational and cultural centre near Şirince, occupying approximately **37,500 square metres** on the slopes of Kayser Mountain. The three villages are physically integrated rather than being entirely separate institutions, with some buildings and facilities shared between mathematics, philosophy and art programmes.
The Mathematics Village continues to run high-school, undergraduate and graduate programmes. Its 2026 undergraduate and graduate summer camp runs from **27 July to 27 September 2026**, with participants studying mathematics alongside academics from Turkey and elsewhere. The programme also continues the Village's communal model, with participants expected to contribute to everyday tasks such as cooking, cleaning, gardening and dishwashing.
Participation is not necessarily free in the literal sense: programmes can charge fees for accommodation, meals and basic services. However, the organisation maintains that **no student should be excluded from mathematics camps simply because they cannot afford the fee**, and it operates a fee-waiver/support system based on financial need.
The Village therefore combines several forms of commons-based practice: volunteer teaching, shared physical work, collective maintenance, non-profit organisation, financial support for participants, and an educational philosophy centred on intellectual freedom rather than credentials.
==Significance==
The Nesin Villages represent an unusual experiment in **decentralised, community-based education**. Their importance lies not simply in providing mathematics, philosophy or arts courses, but in attempting to create a physical and social environment in which education becomes a shared activity.
The Village effectively functions as a small-scale educational commons: teachers contribute knowledge, students contribute labour and participation, volunteers contribute time and expertise, and the physical infrastructure is maintained collectively. Its model challenges the assumption that serious education must necessarily take place within conventional universities, schools or commercial training institutions.
Its continuing existence also demonstrates the possibility of maintaining an independent educational institution outside the conventional examination and credential system while connecting local students with an international community of academics, artists and researchers.
=More information=
* [[Educational Commons]]
External links
* Nesin Villages — https://nesinkoyleri.org/en/main-page/ * Nesin Mathematics Village — https://nesinkoyleri.org/en/main-page/nesin-maths-village/ * Nesin Philosophy Village — https://nesinkoyleri.org/en/main-page/nesin-philosophy-village/ * Nesin Art Village — https://nesinartvillage.org/ * Nesin Foundation — https://nesinvakfi.org/ * Ali Nesin — https://www.alinesin.org/ * Nesin Mathematics Village — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nesin_Mathematics_Village * Ali Nesin's Leelavati Prize lecture — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XI4RwMmLQHQ

'''= "a term coined by Brad deGraf'''" [https://kevintriplett.substack.com/p/the-candili-collective-greece?] URL = https://hackmd.io/8VhGzc-kQsidKZXo-0RsgQ? NAO asks: ''How can networks of peers become capable of continuously sensing, learning and adapting together?'' The NAO is therefore not necessarily a new institutional form. It is better understood as a '''pattern of organization''' that P2P networks may develop. =Definition= A working definition is: '''"A Networked Adaptive Organism is a distributed collective of autonomous human, organizational and/or computational agents whose relationships, shared information, trust mechanisms and feedback loops enable the network to sense, learn, coordinate and adapt as a whole while preserving the sovereignty of its participants."''' The important distinction is that the "organism" is not necessarily a new legal or institutional entity. It is an '''emergent capacity of the network'''. =Description= Entry from DeepSeek, prompted by Michel Bauwens and inspired by Kevin Triplett: < " '''Commons provide the shared resources and purpose; P2P provides the relational architecture; NAO provides adaptive collective capacity." ''' > '''Networked Adaptive Organism''' ('''NAO''') is a concept developed by [[Brad deGraf]] to describe a new form of collective organization in which autonomous people, organizations, communities and potentially machine agents form a network that can collectively '''sense, learn, coordinate and adapt''' while preserving the autonomy of its participants. The concept combines the distributed nature of a [[Peer to Peer]] network with the adaptive characteristics of a living system. Rather than treating an organization as a fixed hierarchy or a network as merely a collection of connections, the NAO proposes that relationships between autonomous agents can generate an emergent collective capacity — a kind of [[Collective Intelligence]]. The term is still evolving and does not yet have a single universally accepted definition. It is therefore best understood as an '''organizational pattern''' or '''design hypothesis''' rather than as a formally established institutional category. A useful distinction is: '''[[DAO]]:''' decentralizes organizational rules and ownership. '''NAO:''' seeks to cultivate adaptive collective intelligence. = Characteristics = The term can be understood through its three components: === Networked === Intelligence and capacity are distributed across relationships rather than concentrated in a central authority. A networked system allows different participants to possess different knowledge, capabilities and resources while remaining connected through shared protocols, information and relationships. == Adaptive == The system can respond to changing conditions. Adaptation requires feedback. A NAO should be capable of: * sensing changes in its environment * interpreting distributed information * experimenting with responses * learning from outcomes * changing its behavior * reorganizing relationships when necessary Adaptation therefore implies a continuous cycle: '''Sense → Make sense → Decide → Act → Learn → Adapt''' == Organism == "Organism" is used as a metaphor for an integrated, living system rather than as a claim that a network is literally a biological organism. A biological organism consists of differentiated components that retain local functions while participating in a larger system. Its capabilities emerge through interaction between those components. A NAO proposes an analogous possibility for social systems: '''Autonomous agents + relationships + feedback + shared purpose → emergent collective capacity''' The organism therefore exists primarily at the level of '''relationships and interactions'''. =Details= == From network to organism == Not every network is an organism. A social network may connect thousands of people while producing very little collective intelligence. The distinctive proposition of the NAO is that a sufficiently well-designed network can develop mechanisms for: * sensing * memory * coordination * learning * adaptation * collective action The transition can be expressed conceptually as: '''Network → Network with feedback → Learning network → Adaptive network → Networked organism''' This is not necessarily a linear developmental sequence. Different networks may exhibit some of these properties without exhibiting others. == Autonomy and interdependence == A central principle of the NAO concept is the coexistence of '''individual sovereignty''' and '''collective intelligence'''. Participants should not have to surrender their autonomy in order to contribute to the collective. Instead, autonomy becomes a source of diversity and resilience. Different participants may contribute: * knowledge * experience * relationships * resources * skills * creativity * local intelligence * judgment * computational capacity The collective becomes more capable precisely because participants are not identical. This produces an important distinction: '''Coordination does not necessarily require command.''' A NAO may coordinate through: * trust * reputation * shared information * protocols * consent * reciprocity * distributed decision-making * negotiated commitments * continuous feedback == Trust as infrastructure == In hierarchical organizations, coordination can often be enforced through authority, contracts and formal procedures. A distributed adaptive system requires additional forms of infrastructure. '''Trust becomes a coordination technology.''' Trust enables participants to: * collaborate with incomplete information * delegate without surrendering sovereignty * share resources * rely on distributed expertise * make commitments across organizational boundaries * cooperate without requiring central approval for every action This suggests that a NAO requires not only technical infrastructure but also '''social infrastructure'''. Such infrastructure can include: * identity * reputation * provenance * transparency * consent * accountability * conflict resolution * shared memory * norms * governance protocols == Collective intelligence == A NAO is not simply a crowd and not merely a large database. Its intelligence emerges from the '''interaction between participants'''. Collective intelligence becomes possible when: * information can circulate * participants can discover one another * different perspectives can interact * knowledge can be recombined * contributions can be attributed * feedback is available * decisions can be revised * learning remains accessible to the network The NAO can therefore be understood as an '''architecture for collective learning'''. == The adaptive loop == A useful model for a Networked Adaptive Organism is: 
       ┌──────────────┐
       │    SENSE     │
       └──────┬───────┘
              ↓
       ┌──────────────┐
       │  MAKE SENSE  │
       └──────┬───────┘
              ↓
       ┌──────────────┐
       │    DECIDE    │
       └──────┬───────┘
              ↓
       ┌──────────────┐
       │     ACT      │
       └──────┬───────┘
              ↓
       ┌──────────────┐
       │    LEARN     │
       └──────┬───────┘
              ↓
       ┌──────────────┐
       │    ADAPT     │
       └──────┬───────┘
              │
              └──────────────→ SENSE
The crucial property is the '''closed feedback loop'''. Without learning, a network is merely coordinated. Without adaptation, it is merely organized. A NAO is intended to remain capable of changing itself in response to experience. == Memory == An adaptive organism needs memory. For a social network, memory can include: * decisions * agreements * relationships * contributions * experiments * failures * successful practices * institutional knowledge * provenance * cultural knowledge Digital infrastructure can make this collective memory more persistent and searchable. This raises an important distinction between conventional organizations and NAOs: '''Organizational memory does not have to belong to an institution. It can belong to the network.''' This is particularly relevant to P2P systems, where knowledge can remain available even when individual projects or organizations disappear. == Agency == A NAO can be thought of as having multiple levels of agency: * individual agency * group agency * network agency * ecosystem agency The existence of network-level agency does not necessarily imply the disappearance of individual agency. Instead, the proposition is that: '''individual agency + relational agency → collective agency''' This is one of the central philosophical questions raised by the concept. == Human and machine agents == Contemporary NAOs may include both human and computational agents. Humans contribute: * lived experience * values * judgment * creativity * relationships * embodied knowledge * ethical responsibility Software and AI agents may contribute: * information processing * pattern recognition * simulation * memory * matching * translation * coordination * continuous monitoring In this model, AI can become part of the '''nervous system of the network''' without becoming the owner or sovereign of the network. A useful design principle is: '''Technology should augment the agency of participants rather than absorb it.''' == Polycentricity and nested networks == A NAO does not necessarily imply one enormous network. Instead, NAOs may be '''nested'''. For example: '''Person → Team → Community → Territory → Network of territories → Planetary network''' Each level can retain a degree of autonomy while participating in larger systems. This resembles [[Polycentric Governance]] and other forms of federated organization. The resulting architecture may be described as '''fractal''': * autonomous local units * connected through interoperable relationships * capable of forming larger temporary or persistent wholes * without requiring a single center == Territorial applications == The NAO concept may be particularly relevant to territorial transition. A territory may contain: * farmers * municipalities * cooperatives * associations * businesses * citizens * researchers * ecological initiatives * cultural organizations * infrastructure providers These actors may already be individually effective while remaining poorly connected. A NAO approach asks: ''What if the relationships between these initiatives were treated as infrastructure?'' This shifts the focus from building isolated projects to building '''territorial capacity'''. The objective becomes the ability of a territory to: * perceive its own conditions * share knowledge * mobilize distributed resources * coordinate initiatives * learn collectively * respond to shocks * regenerate itself == Network weaving == One practical implication is the importance of '''network weaving'''. Network weaving means actively creating and strengthening relationships between people and organizations that would otherwise remain disconnected. In a NAO, network weaving can function as a form of connective tissue. The network does not become adaptive merely because connections exist. Connections need to become: * meaningful * reciprocal * information-rich * trusted * actionable =Governance= A NAO requires governance, but governance does not necessarily mean hierarchy. Possible governance mechanisms include: * consent * distributed authority * delegated authority * rotating roles * reputation * peer accountability * transparent decision records * federated decision-making * constitutional principles * conflict transformation The key question is not: ''How do we eliminate governance?'' but: ''How do we govern a system whose participants remain autonomous and whose configuration is continuously changing?'' =Resilience= A major potential advantage of the NAO architecture is resilience. Centralized systems can be efficient but vulnerable to failures at critical points. A distributed system may have greater redundancy because knowledge, capability and relationships exist in multiple locations. However, decentralization does not automatically produce resilience. A NAO can become fragile through: * poor coordination * information overload * trust failures * fragmentation * governance capture * incompatible protocols * lack of shared purpose Resilience therefore depends on the quality of the network's relationships and feedback mechanisms. =Status= The term is increasingly being used in practical experiments. In 2025, an international team brought together by [[Allelo]] worked on a prototype Networked Adaptive Organism focused on digital sovereignty. The project explored a decentralized trust layer in which identity, data and community relationships could support collective intelligence and decision-making. ([https://luma.com/03njsz16 Luma — "NAO or Never!" community call]) The Open Co-op reports that Oliver Sylvester-Bradley collaborated with an international team brought together by Allelo in 2025 to prototype the first NAO, including development of a distributed network graph built on [[NextGraph]]. ([https://open.coop/oliver-sylvester-bradley/ The Open Co-op — Oliver Sylvester-Bradley]) Other current projects are experimenting with NAOs as cooperative governance structures and with AI-supported infrastructure and collective decision-making. ([https://www.tesseractstakes.com/pathways/ Tesseract — Pathways]) These projects should be regarded as '''experiments and implementations of an emerging concept''', rather than definitive embodiments of NAO. == Brad deGraf == '''Brad deGraf''' is associated with the development of the Networked Adaptive Organism concept. His earlier work explored social networks, collective decision-making and technologies for enabling distributed intelligence. This provides an important background to the NAO proposition: the network is not merely a communications layer but can become a medium through which collective judgment and action emerge. =More information= == External links == * [https://open.coop/oliver-sylvester-bradley/ The Open Co-op — Oliver Sylvester-Bradley] * [https://luma.com/03njsz16 Luma — "NAO or Never!" community call] * [https://www.tesseractstakes.com/pathways/ Tesseract — Pathways] [[Category:Network Theory]] [[Category:Commons]] [[Category:Intelligence]]

page.title: Self-Organizing Evolution as a Source of Meaning

revision.comment: /* Integrated Worldview */
revision.text:
'''* Article: Heylighen, F., Beigi, S., & Vidal, C. (in press). The Third Story of the Universe: self-organizing evolution as a source of meaning. Foundations of Science. 2026'''
URL = https://cris.vub.be/ws/portalfiles/portal/281521855/Third_Story-working_paper-submitt.pdf?
=Abstract=
"We introduce and elaborate a new, evolutionary worldview, as a “Third Story”, intended to replace and complement the earlier religious (First) and mechanistic (Second) worldviews.
The confusions created by a world that is ever more volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous have eroded people’s “sense of coherence”, i.e. the degree to which they experience the world as comprehensible, manageable and meaningful.
* The First Story provides meaning and values, but its descriptions no longer provide an accurate understanding of the universe.
* The Second Story, which sees the universe as a clockwork mechanism governed by the laws of nature, provides more accurate predictions that allow us to build powerful technologies. However, it does not provide meaning or values.
* The Third Story sees the universe as self-organizing towards increasing complexity and consciousness, subsequently producing matter, life, mind and society. It understands the fundamental mechanism of evolution as mutual adaptation between interacting systems, thus generating synergetic wholes that in turn interact, so as integrate into even more complex wholes. Its implicit value is the search for fitness and synergy, thus inviting individuals to work towards a further evolutionary integration into the noosphere, i.e. the planetary superorganism formed by humanity, its technological extensions, and the ecosystem."
=Excerpts=
==[[Sense of Coherence]]==
Francis Heylighen et al. :
"Coined by the sociologist Aaron Antonovsky, the SOC concept denotes a broad, constructive attitude about life and the world in which one lives.
It is composed of three aspects (Antonovsky 1998; Eriksson and Lindström 2006):
(1) comprehensibility: people have a general understanding of how the world functions and which things may or may not happen to them.
(2) manageability: people feel they have the necessary (individual or social) resources and skills that would allow them to cope with conceivable challenges.
(3) meaningfulness: people have goals and values that they consider worth striving for.
A wide variety of studies have established that individuals with a higher sense of coherence can deal better with life’s challenges, traumas and stressors (Antonovsky 1998; Eriksson and Lindström 2006). SOC provides a comprehensive and enduring way of making sense of the world. The stronger a person’s SOC, the more likely the person will be able to cope successfully with stress, anxiety, and despair (Carlén et al. 2020; Eriksson 2017). The SOC model assumes that individuals actively participate in shaping their understanding and formulating an empowering life narrative. In other words, individuals with a strong SOC are able to identify relevant coping resources, to effectively utilize these resources, and to derive emotionally significant lessons when faced with unfortunate life events. Such proactive engagement connects individuals' concrete actions with the way they make sense of the world in which they live."
(https://cris.vub.be/ws/portalfiles/portal/281521855/Third_Story-working_paper-submitt.pdf?)
==[[Integrated Worldview]]==
Shima Beigi et al. :
" This is a broad conceptual scheme that helps people orient themselves in the world and find meaning in what happens to them (Park 2010; Steger 2009). In the tradition initiated by the philosopher Leo Apostel, an integrated worldview can be seen as consisting of six components that form a coherent framework (Aerts et al. 1994; Vidal 2012; 2008). These components can be understood as fundamental aspects or dimensions of meaning.
Whenever we are confronted with a situation or phenomenon that we need to make sense of, we will tend to ask the following questions:
(1) Present (Identification): what is it? What precisely is going on?
(2) Past (Explanation): where does it come from? Why is it there? What caused it to be?
(3) Future (Prediction): where is it going to? What are the likely consequences?
(4) Knowledge: do I have the necessary facts? How can I find out more?
(5) Action: how can I deal with the situation? What courses of action do I have?
(6) Value: what are the good and the bad aspects? Which goals should I try to achieve?
The first three aspects are “objective”: they focus on understanding the external situation. The last three are subjective: they try to clarify the relation between the subject (“I”) and the situation, so that the subject knows how to react. This worldview scheme can be understood as an extension of Antonovsky’s three-component [[Sence of Coherence]] scheme."
(https://cris.vub.be/ws/portalfiles/portal/281521855/Third_Story-working_paper-submitt.pdf?)

=Source=
'''* Article: Seeing Through the Paradigm: Understanding the Living Architecture of Belief. By Ernesto Van Peborgh, aug 08, 2026'''
URL = https://substack.com/home/post/p-210367668?
=Context=
Ernesto van Peborgh:
"Every paradigm that has ever existed began as a small handful of relationships capable of imagining reality otherwise, and so did every civilization; and ours, it may be, already has begun. Not because the old paradigm has vanished — it has not, and like every living system it will go on defending the coherence that once let it thrive, for a long while yet. But underneath its familiar structures another pattern is rooting, one that measures wealth not only by what can be pulled out of the world but by what can be endlessly renewed within it, that understands resilience not as resistance to change but as the capacity to evolve with it, and that recognizes, at last, that the deepest infrastructure of every economy and every society and every future is the living world itself.
Whether that pattern grows is not, in the end, a question history will settle on our behalf. It is answered instead in a quieter register, every day, in the relationships each of us chooses to cultivate or to neglect — which means the future is not waiting somewhere ahead of us, finished and inevitable, for us to walk toward.
Like every living system that has ever come into being, it is already beginning, right now, in the space between us."
(https://substack.com/home/post/p-210367668?)
=Discussion=
(Selections from the full article, focused on the process of Paradigm Change)
==The Immune System of the Old Paradigm==
Ernesto van Peborgh:
"A living body does not passively wait to be harmed. It patrols itself. It keeps a standing capacity to recognize what does not belong and to move against it before the intrusion can spread, and this immune vigilance is not a defect of the organism but one of the surest signs that the organism is alive and intends to stay that way.
A paradigm, if it is genuinely a living system, should possess something of the same. It does. Watch closely during any real contest of worldviews and you will see the immune system of an idea come awake. Its first and gentlest response is simply not to perceive.
Don’t Look Up offered a brilliant satire of something much deeper than climate denial: our extraordinary capacity to receive information that threatens the assumptions of our prevailing paradigm and somehow translate it back into something the paradigm can accommodate. The scientists are describing physical reality; the television hosts keep translating that reality into the familiar grammar of entertainment, reassurance, and normality. Nothing is hidden. The information is right there. And yet, somehow, it cannot quite be seen.
The unassimilable observation arrives and finds no receptor waiting for it, and so it is filed under noise, anecdote, coincidence, the merely subjective — set gently aside, not with malice but with the quiet confidence of a system that already knows what the real signals look like.
For decades the small farmers reporting that their living soils outperformed their chemically managed neighbors’ were heard, when they were heard at all, as folklore, sincere and unquantified and therefore safely ignorable. The data existed. The receptors did not. When an intrusion grows too large to overlook, the immune response escalates from silence into naming, and the naming is rarely kind.
The disruptive idea is labeled — romantic, unscientific, nostalgic, naïve, ideological, unrealistic — and each of these labels performs the same protective work, which is to spare the community the trouble of actually metabolizing the thing. To call an idea nostalgic is to explain, without argument, why one need not think about it.
The antibody has done its job: the threat is neutralized not by being answered but by being categorized in a way that makes an answer feel unnecessary. Should the idea keep growing despite the labels, the system reaches for its most sophisticated defense of all, and this one deserves our respect for its cunning. It absorbs the language of the challenger while leaving the challenger’s meaning at the door. The words are welcomed in; the world they came from is turned away. Sustainability enters the vocabulary of the very industries busy liquidating the future and is quietly redefined to mean sustaining present rates of extraction a little longer. Regenerative becomes a label on a package, a claim on a quarterly report, a marketing surface stretched over an unchanged machine.
This is not usually hypocrisy in the crude sense; it is immunity in its most refined form, the paradigm neutralizing a foreign meaning by keeping the sound of the word and digesting away everything the word was trying to carry. We are tempted to feel superior to all this, to imagine that our own convictions arise from clear looking while other people’s arise from defended illusion.
That temptation is worth resisting, because the immune response is not something that afflicts other people’s paradigms. It is running in each of us, right now, doing its patient work at the edge of our attention, deciding what we will be able to hear before we ever hear it. The honest question is never whether we have an immune system. It is whether we can catch it in the act.
==Where a New Way of Seeing Actually Comes From==
If paradigms defend themselves so effectively — if they can decline to perceive, decline to take seriously, and even digest the words of their successors — then it becomes a genuine puzzle how anything new ever manages to arrive at all.
And the answer is that it almost never arrives where the defenses are strongest. New paradigms are not, as a rule, born at the center of the old one. They are not usually the achievement of its most decorated authorities, whose seeing has been most thoroughly formed by the coherence now under strain. They tend to begin at the edges, in the places and among the people for whom the old coherence was already failing to account for a lived and undeniable experience.
There is an ecology to this, and it is worth naming plainly. In a forest, the most vigorous new growth rarely erupts in the deep shade of the oldest, densest, most established canopy, where everything is already spoken for and every ray of light already claimed. It comes at the edge — the forest’s margin, the burned clearing, the fallen giant whose collapse has suddenly let light reach the floor.
Ecologists call these edges and openings the sites of the highest diversity and the fastest change, and cultures obey a strikingly similar law. The next way of seeing tends to take root among those the current paradigm has failed, overlooked, or could never quite hold: the practitioners whose direct experience keeps contradicting the official account, the young who have not yet been fully enclosed inside the inherited common sense, the outsiders standing at enough of an angle to notice the water.
This is why the emergence of a paradigm so seldom looks like emergence while it is happening. It does not announce itself with a manifesto or a single decisive experiment. It looks, from the center, like scattered noise — a handful of farmers doing something eccentric with cover crops, a cluster of scientists chasing questions that seem to lead nowhere the field values, a fringe of communities organizing their economies around principles the textbooks never taught.
Each fragment is easy to dismiss on its own, and each is duly dismissed. What the center cannot see, precisely because its coherence forbids the seeing, is that these scattered fragments are beginning, slowly, to find one another — to recognize a shared pattern beneath their surface differences, to build the connective tissue through which isolated anomalies gradually become a coherent alternative way of understanding the world.
And here the living metaphor turns from consolation into something more demanding. A seed carries the whole information of the forest, but it germinates only where conditions permit — where there is light enough, moisture enough, the right disturbance in the soil.
A new paradigm is much the same. Its seeds may already be everywhere, dormant, patient, distributed far more widely than anyone at the center suspects. What determines whether they grow is not the brilliance of the seed but the readiness of the ground: whether enough people have suffered the failures of the old coherence deeply enough to become, at last, hospitable soil.
==The Long Middle, Where Two Worlds Overlap==
We would prefer our transitions clean. We would like the old world to finish and the new one to begin, with a clear seam between them we could point to and date. But that is almost never how a paradigm actually gives way to its successor, and the gap between the transition we imagine and the transition we get is the source of a great deal of our present bewilderment. What really happens is a long, disorienting middle in which both worlds are fully present at once — the old paradigm still structuring most of our institutions, still writing most of our laws, still holding most of the money and nearly all of the momentum, while the new one grows up through its cracks, unevenly, in patches, real but not yet dominant.
This overlap is not comfortable, and it is not supposed to be. It is a season in which the same word means opposite things to different people, in which an action that is obviously responsible inside one paradigm looks obviously reckless from inside the other, in which institutions built entirely on the old coherence are asked to steward a world their instruments can no longer accurately read. A great deal of what we experience as political dysfunction is, at bottom, this overlap made visible — not simply a fight between interests, though it is also that, but a collision between two ways of perceiving what is even at stake, two incompatible answers to the prior question of what the situation is.
I have explored this transitional space extensively through the framework of the Three Horizons.
Ecosystems know this season and pass through it without panic. When a landscape shifts from one stable state toward another — grassland easing into woodland, a degraded field beginning its slow return toward forest — there is a long interval in which the community is genuinely mixed, the pioneers of the coming order growing alongside the holdouts of the old, no single logic yet in command of the whole.
Ecologists do not read this as failure or as chaos. They read it as succession: the entirely lawful, if untidy, process by which one living configuration hands the world over to the next. It cannot be hurried into tidiness, and the attempt to force it — to declare the transition already complete, or to insist it is not happening at all — tends only to prolong the disorder.
What the overlap asks of anyone living through it is a peculiar and difficult double vision: the capacity to see the old paradigm clearly enough to work within it where one still must, to keep the lights on and the harvests coming and the institutions functioning, while simultaneously seeing the new one clearly enough to feed it, to give it soil and light and one’s own daily participation.
This is not fence-sitting and it is not lukewarm compromise. It is the specific labor of a threshold, the work of people who understand that they are living in the seam between worlds and have decided to make themselves useful there rather than pretending the seam does not run straight through their own lives.
...
==Tending the Conditions Rather Than Forcing the Result==
There is a way of trying to change the world that belongs entirely to the old paradigm even when it is aimed at the new one, and it is worth learning to recognize, because a great deal of sincere effort is quietly wasted on it.
It is the engineer’s posture applied to living things — the assumption that transformation is a matter of sufficient force correctly aimed, that if we could only design the right policy, build the right technology, win the right argument, or seize the right levers, we could install a new paradigm the way one installs a new machine.
The intention is often admirable. The underlying picture is the very mechanism the new paradigm was supposed to leave behind.
A gardener knows something the engineer’s posture cannot quite absorb, and it is this: you cannot force a plant to grow. You can pull at a seedling all afternoon and succeed only in killing it.
What a gardener actually does is far humbler and, in the end, far more powerful — she tends the conditions from which growth becomes possible and then extends to the living thing the one courtesy the engineer never learned to offer, which is trust in a process she did not design and does not control. She builds the soil, adjusts the light, sees to the water, removes what crowds, and then she waits, participating in a growth whose real agency belongs to the plant and not to her.
The whole art lies in the distinction between making something happen and cultivating the conditions under which it can happen on its own.
Everything in this essay points toward the second posture and away from the first. If a paradigm is a living system, then it cannot be installed, only cultivated — which relocates the real work of transition from the grand and distant levers we mostly cannot reach to the near and ordinary ground we touch every day.
The conditions from which a new paradigm grows are not, finally, abstract. They are the actual quality of our conversations, in which a different way of seeing is either given air or quietly suffocated. They are the design of the organizations we build, the questions we permit ourselves to ask, the relationships we choose to enter and how we choose to hold them. Each of these is soil. Each is a place where the next paradigm becomes, by some small increment, more alive or less.
This reframing is a relief and a responsibility in equal measure. It is a relief because it releases us from the exhausting and slightly grandiose fantasy that the future depends on our personally winning some decisive and total victory.
And it is a responsibility because it removes the more comfortable fantasy on the other side — that transformation is someone else’s job, happening elsewhere, at a scale too large for our small hands to matter.
If paradigms grow the way living things grow, then they grow through the daily tending of ordinary people in ordinary places, or they do not grow at all. There turns out to be no one else. There is only the soil in front of each of us, and what we are willing to do with it."
(https://substack.com/home/post/p-210367668?)

=Discussion=
==The Three Crises for Free Will==
Albert Yuan:
"The question of free will has survived three major crises in Western intellectual history, each one threatening to extinguish it entirely.
The first was in ancient Greece, roughly 2,500 years ago, when philosophers like Democritus and Leucippus looked at the world with admirable rigor and concluded that everything — atoms bouncing in a void, future events — was already determined. The first crack: determinism. The second crack: the causal chain. Your choice of breakfast traces back not to you but to your caffeine dependency, which traces to your addiction-prone neurobiology, which traces to your parents, which traces to the emergence of mammals, which traces to the birth of the solar system. At some point, the causal thread escapes your body entirely.
The second crisis emerged with monotheism. If God is omniscient and omnipotent, in what sense are human choices genuinely free? St. Augustine answered with characteristic ingenuity: God gave us the freedom to choose good, but our ancestors squandered it in the Garden of Eden. Thomas Aquinas deepened the synthesis, positioning God as the “first cause” and human rational agency as a “second cause” — not in conflict, but nested. For centuries, this reconciliation held.
The third crisis is the one we are still living through, and it is the most democratized of the three. It began with Newton, accelerated through Darwin and has now arrived, via neuroscience, in everyone’s living room. The physicist showed us a clockwork universe. The biologist showed us that organisms are the undesigned products of genetic mutation and natural selection. And neuroscience — particularly one elegantly simple experiment — showed us something that feels, to many people, like the final blow."
(https://www.noemamag.com/the-nature-of-free-will-in-the-age-of-ai/?)

=Description=
Will Ruddick:
"An attempt to make some of these relationships visible:
Who is contributing to a local economy?
What kinds of value are entering and leaving?
Are local commitments circulating among people, or only accumulating?
When national currency enters a community, does it replace local exchange, support it, or move alongside it?
How do separate savings groups begin to form a wider economic network without giving up their own rules?
...
The visualizer reconstructs 4,606 public Celo transaction events from 9 January through 13 August 2026. It connects these transactions with public information about pools, community vouchers, marketplace offers, and field reports.
A Chama (mutual-aid group) is not only an account holding money. It is a group of people making commitments to one another.
Each pool can decide which vouchers (commitments for goods and services) it accepts, how it values them, how much it will hold, and what it will offer in exchange. These decisions create a curated marketplace rather than an unrestricted pool of interchangeable assets.
One pool might hold commitments for food, transport, farm work, construction, or other goods and services alongside stable currencies. Another pool can make different choices.
The five pools remain distinct, but some of their vouchers can move between them. This begins to look like a cosmo-local federation: local groups keeping their own boundaries while sharing enough infrastructure for value to travel."
(https://willruddick.substack.com/p/bioregional-cosmo-local-credit-flows?)
=Discussion=
Will Ruddick:
" What interests me is not simply that blockchain transactions can be animated.
I am interested in whether communities can see and govern the relationship between their productive capacity, their commitments to one another, and the national currency moving through their region.
These five Chamas combine savings-like contributions, external stable funding, reciprocal commitments, pool-mediated exchange, direct voucher movement, public offers, and community activity.
Each pool keeps its own curation, valuation, limits, inventory, and right to say no.
Shared assets make coordination across pools possible.
At a village scale, this can help a group understand its own commitments and liquidity.
At a bioregional scale, connected pools could show how food, labor, transport, care, energy, and national currency circulate among communities.
At a larger public scale, similar tools could help institutions ask whether finance is strengthening local productive capacity or extracting from it.
The visualizer does not answer those questions by itself.
A ledger can preserve a mistaken account. A protocol can execute a harmful rule perfectly. A beautiful map can make weak assumptions look more certain than they are.
The purpose is not to replace judgment.
It is to make relationships inspectable enough that communities, researchers, and public institutions can ask better questions together."
